1	---
2	prev-chapter: "NLP for HCLLMs"
3	prev-url: "04-nlp.html"
4	page-title: Evaluations for HCLLMs
5	search-title: "Chapter 5: Evaluations for HCLLMs"
6	next-chapter: "Responsible Human-Centered LLMs"
7	next-url: "06-responsible.html"
8	---
9	# Evaluation
10	
11	[]{#sec:evaluation label="sec:evaluation"}
12	
13	Evaluation methods allow model developers, users, and stakeholders to
14	compare the capabilities and limitations of different LLMs, and to
15	understand the scope of their utilities and risks in particular domains
16	[@10.1145/3641289]. Evaluations can inform all stages of model
17	development, from mixing pre-training data
18	[@held2025optimizing; @mizrahi2025language] to selecting and optimizing
19	reward models for alignment
20	[@lambert2024rewardbenchevaluatingrewardmodels; @frick2024evaluate].
21	After models are trained, evaluations arguably become even more
22	important. They act quality filters to decide whether and how companies
23	deploy models [@liang2022holistic]. They inform researchers on the most
24	important and promising directions for model improvement
25	[@srivastava2022beyond], and help anticipate models' future capabilities
26	[@kaplan2020scaling; @hoffmann2022training]. And finally, they shape
27	public perceptions [@liao2022designing], and inform policy and other
28	regulatory decisions [@eriksson2025can].
29	
30	Without a human-centered evaluation of LLMs, model development,
31	deployment, and governance may be oriented not towards the long-term and
32	collective good, but rather towards profit incentives and short-term
33	gains on surface-level heuristics [@eriksson2025can]. In this chapter,
34	we observe common pitfalls and highlight best practices in
35	human-centered evaluation, spanning three levels as shown in
36	Figure [1](#fig:evaluation){reference-type="ref"
37	reference="fig:evaluation"}. First, we consider evaluations at the level
38	of model outputs
39	([\[subsec:model_level_eval\]](#subsec:model_level_eval){reference-type="ref"
40	reference="subsec:model_level_eval"}), using both quantitative metrics
41	([5.5.2](#subsub:quantitative_methods){reference-type="ref"
42	reference="subsub:quantitative_methods"}) and qualitative evaluations
43	([5.5.3](#subsub:qualitative_evaluation){reference-type="ref"
44	reference="subsub:qualitative_evaluation"}). Beyond raw outputs, we also
45	consider how people experience LLMs
46	([\[subsec:human_centered_eval\]](#subsec:human_centered_eval){reference-type="ref"
47	reference="subsec:human_centered_eval"}), considering human values
48	([5.2.1](#subsub:human_values){reference-type="ref"
49	reference="subsub:human_values"}), as well as concerns over bias
50	([\[subsec:bias_eval\]](#subsec:bias_eval){reference-type="ref"
51	reference="subsec:bias_eval"}) and safety
52	([\[subsec:safety_eval\]](#subsec:safety_eval){reference-type="ref"
53	reference="subsec:safety_eval"}). Lastly, we discuss extrinsic
54	evaluations at the societal level
55	([\[subsec:impact\]](#subsec:impact){reference-type="ref"
56	reference="subsec:impact"}), measuring the system's real world impact.
57	
58	![In this chapter, we discuss common pitfalls and best practices for
59	evaluating HCLLMs, considering three distinct levels of evaluation: the
60	model level
61	([\[subsec:model_level_eval\]](#subsec:model_level_eval){reference-type="ref"
62	reference="subsec:model_level_eval"}), the human level
63	([\[subsec:human_centered_eval\]](#subsec:human_centered_eval){reference-type="ref"
64	reference="subsec:human_centered_eval"}), and the societal level
65	([\[subsec:impact\]](#subsec:impact){reference-type="ref"
66	reference="subsec:impact"}).](../assets/sec5.png){#fig:evaluation
67	width="\\linewidth"}
68	
69	## Model-Level Evaluations
70	
71	[]{#subsec:model_level_eval label="subsec:model_level_eval"}
72	
73	### Benchmarks
74	
75	[]{#subsec:benchmarks label="subsec:benchmarks"}
76	
77	Benchmarking has long been a key driver in the development of AI
78	systems. Benchmarks act as a compass, encoding the values, priorities,
79	and goals of the AI research community
80	[@ethayarajh2020utility; @birhane2022values]. They help determine not
81	only how capable a model is, but also what we consider meaningful
82	progress, allowing us to compare the strengths of different models.
83	Recent research has argued for a shift in what and how we evaluate,
84	especially for human-centered applications. As LLMs increasingly
85	influence real-world decision-making, especially in domains like
86	education, law, healthcare, and customer support, the limitations of
87	traditional benchmarks become even more critical. Benchmarks must evolve
88	to better represent human values such as fairness, robustness,
89	usability, and positive societal impact. Below, we discuss a few general
90	principles for thinking about evaluating human-centered LLMs.
91	
92	#### Moving Away from \"Exams\" and Rethinking What We Evaluate.
93	
94	Traditional benchmarks often mimic academic exams, assessing LLMs by how
95	well they can replicate human outputs or solve static problems in
96	standardized formats like multiple-choice questions
97	[@hendrycksMMLU2021], math problems [@sun2025challenging], and code
98	generation [@jimenezswe]. While useful, this framing compresses complex,
99	multidimensional model behavior into a single metric. Even
100	interaction-based, human-voting evaluations like ChatbotArena
101	[@DBLP:conf/icml/ChiangZ0ALLZ0JG24] are limited by their brittleness or
102	their misalignment with how humans actually use AI
103	[@singh2025leaderboard]. In real-world use, LLMs are collaborators,
104	copilots, or tools embedded in workflows, so it becomes necessary to
105	evaluate them in natural, complex, and multi-step human-AI interaction
106	settings, not just in isolation. One promising alternative is centaur
107	evaluations [@haupt2025ai] where humans and models collaborate. Here, we
108	care about the outcome of the combined system. These setups get closer
109	to how AI is actually used in practice, whether it's writing, analysis,
110	customer support, diagnosis, or decision-making.
111	
112	#### Ecological Validity.
113	
114	A central challenge in evaluating LLMs for real-world use is ecological
115	validity, the extent to which a benchmark setting reflects the
116	complexity of how systems are actually used. Controlled evaluations may
117	offer cleaner signals, but they often fail to generalize to interactive,
118	user-facing deployments. Recent work [@li2025mind] has shown that no
119	single benchmark strongly correlates with interactive performance for
120	audio models across 20 existing datasets. A model that excels at
121	standard static tasks might still struggle in dynamic or collaborative
122	environments. This mismatch suggests a need for richer, context-aware
123	evaluations. One promising direction is to build evaluations bottom-up
124	from in-the-wild data. For example, @rottger2025issuebench evaluate
125	perspective and framing biases in LLM responses to natural user queries.
126	Benchmarks should also be robust and reliable, correlating good
127	performance with success in real tasks. This requires vetted examples
128	with accurate annotations and sufficient statistical power
129	[@bowman2021will]. Finally, effective benchmarks should reveal potential
130	biases, artifacts, and any dual uses, as well as ways to mitigate such
131	unintended consequences [@weidinger2022taxonomy].
132	
133	#### Data Contamination and Dynamic Alternatives.
134	
135	With LLMs trained on massive web-scale corpora, the risk of benchmark
136	contamination has become a serious issue. Many popular benchmarks are at
137	least partially contained in training data, making their validity as
138	evaluation tools less convincing. The line between training and testing
139	becomes blurry, especially for static tasks. This is one benefit of
140	dynamic, evolving benchmarks. Examples like DynaBench
141	[@kiela2021dynabench], Chatbot Arena
142	[@DBLP:conf/icml/ChiangZ0ALLZ0JG24], WebArena [@zhou2023webarena], and
143	WildVision-Arena [@lu2024wildvision] introduce a degree of human
144	involvement that better mirrors real-world interaction. Such dynamic
145	setups are promising for evaluating generalization and interaction
146	aspects and mitigating issues around saturation and contamination.
147	
148	#### General-Purpose vs. Domain-Specific Evaluations.
149	
150	For example, DR Bench [@gao2023dr] assesses LLMs' diagnostic reasoning
151	abilities, PubMedQA [@jin2019pubmedqa] targets biomedical research
152	question-answering, and LegalBench [@guha2024legalbench] is designed for
153	legal reasoning, including statutory interpretation and contract
154	analysis. In education, benchmarks are emerging to evaluate LLMs'
155	effectiveness in providing innovative and meaningful feedback to
156	teachers [@wang2023chatgpt] and emulate expert decision-making in
157	providing tailored math remediation help bridge the gap between
158	technological capability and educational needs
159	[@wang-etal-2024-bridging]. Recently, GDPval measures model performance
160	on economically valuable, real-world tasks across 44 occupations
161	[@openai_gdpval_2025]. These specialized benchmarks provide useful
162	signals that evaluation is grounded in each specific context, offering
163	contextualized and real-world assessment of model performance compared
164	to simply on math and coding tasks. Collaborative efforts across domains
165	are crucial to developing benchmarks that reflect the full complexity of
166	human-LLM interactions and the contexts in which LLM systems are
167	deployed.
168	
169	Overall, a human-centered framework often transcends traditional metrics
170	and benchmarks that continue to prioritize efficiency and profitability
171	above all else. While these measures are useful in providing objective
172	algorithmic reviews on quantitative criteria, they fail to, or sometimes
173	not even attempt to, capture the human factors and societal patterns
174	that are inherently present in these systems.
175	
176	### Quantitative Evaluation {#subsub:quantitative_methods}
177	
178	**Automatic Metrics.** Notably, among automatic metrics, foundational
179	methods have played a critical role in shaping intrinsic evaluations.
180	These metrics provide a systematic way to evaluate model performance
181	through standardized benchmarks, making the evaluation process more
182	efficient and scalable
183	[@10.1145/3485766; @askell2021generallanguageassistantlaboratory; @hu2024unveilingllmevaluationfocused].
184	
185	Metrics like BLEU [@papineni2002bleu] and ROUGE [@lin2004rouge] are
186	valued for their simplicity and reproducibility. However, their
187	shortcomings include reliance on strict token matching, which often
188	penalizes valid paraphrases and fails to capture deeper semantic
189	equivalence [@wieting-etal-2019-beyond]. Even embedding-based metrics
190	like BERTScore [@hanna-bojar-2021-fine] can be fooled by lexical
191	similarity, ranking a more similar incorrect translation higher than a
192	dissimilar but correct one.
193	
194	Generally, quantitative metrics also are limited in addressing other
195	human needs, such as interpretability, latency, cognitive load, and user
196	satisfaction. Optimizing solely for a metric like perplexity can lead to
197	monotonous responses from a language model
198	[@celikyilmaz2021evaluationtextgenerationsurvey], which would be less
199	appealing to a user. In the high-stakes domains such as healthcare,
200	where applications are highly critical, existing metrics have been found
201	to fail to capture trust, personalization, and empathy
202	[@abbasian2024foundation]. Finally, while these metrics may be
203	automatic, they are often not scalable to tasks such as open-ended
204	question answering and complex planning [@gehrmann2023repairing]. These
205	limitations have led to the development of complementary and alternative
206	evaluation methods.
207	
208	**Reference-based Metrics.** Reference-based approaches measure the
209	similarity between the system output and the predefined reference
210	samples, such as cosine similarity
211	[@agarwal2024aisuggestionshomogenizewriting], the E2E benchmark
212	[@banerjee2023benchmarkingllmpoweredchatbots], HUSE
213	[@hashimoto-etal-2019-unifying], and Reward Bench
214	[@lambert2024rewardbenchevaluatingrewardmodels]. These methods maintain
215	the benefits of standardized and objective evaluation for automatic
216	metrics, but they are also limited to the quality of the used standard.
217	For instance, they may be inconsistent or disprove themselves against
218	new references or optimize for closeness to a single gold standard, even
219	if the overall response quality is worse
220	[@nguyen2024referencebasedmetricsdisprovequestion]. For creative tasks,
221	such a gold standard may not even exist.
222	
223	**Machine-learned Metrics.** Machine-learned metrics such as reward
224	models [@ryan2024unintendedimpactsllmalignment] and classifier-based
225	scoring [@shaikh2024rehearsal] show some promise in capturing nuances of
226	human judgment. However, it can be challenging to build pipelines to
227	ground LLMs, such as with specific sources for factual correctness
228	[@tang-etal-2024-minicheck], or to social science theories that reflect
229	human behavior and preferences [@shaikh2024rehearsal]. Additionally,
230	these methods face limitations in generalizing to out-of-distribution
231	settings, particularly in addressing discrepancies in preferences across
232	different groups of people worldwide
233	[@ryan2024unintendedimpactsllmalignment].
234	
235	### Qualitative Evaluation {#subsub:qualitative_evaluation}
236	
237	In contrast to quantitative evaluations
238	([5.5.2](#subsub:quantitative_methods){reference-type="ref"
239	reference="subsub:quantitative_methods"}), qualitative evaluations
240	require a nuanced approach to evaluation as they work directly with
241	humans (or LLMs). They are perhaps more human-centered than automatic or
242	machine-learned metrics due to their subjects, while requiring more
243	careful considerations to design fair and effective evaluations. We
244	first discuss two paradigms of qualitative evaluations, LLM as a Judge
245	and Human Evaluation. We then end the section with a coverage of
246	Extrinsic Evaluation.
247	
248	**LLM-as-a-Judge.** The rise in popularity of LLMs has led to the
249	"LLM-as-a-Judge" paradigm, which caters towards more human-centered
250	systems. Given the cost and subjectivity of human evaluation, LLM
251	evaluation proves to be a feasible alternative, and the results are
252	generally consistent with results from human experts on some tasks
253	[@chiang2023largelanguagemodelsalternative]. Within the LLM judge
254	paradigm, there are various use cases, such as LLM-derived metrics
255	(embedding-based, probabilities, etc.)
256	[@jia-etal-2023-zero; @xie-etal-2023-deltascore], prompting, fine-tuning
257	LLMs with human evaluations
258	[@xu2023instructscoreexplainabletextgeneration; @ke-etal-2024-critiquellm],
259	and human-LLM collaborative evaluations
260	[@gao2024llmbasednlgevaluationcurrent]. More recent methods employ
261	multiple LLMs to engage in multi-agent debates for evaluations and have
262	shown better alignment with human assessment
263	[@chan2023chatevalbetterllmbasedevaluators]. However, LLM-based
264	evaluators exhibit systematic limitations, including self-preference
265	bias [@panickssery2024llmevaluatorsrecognizefavor], where models favor
266	their own outputs, and inconsistent application of evaluation criteria
267	[@hu2024llmbasedevaluatorsconfusingnlg], both of which reduce the
268	reliability of their judgments. One set of limitations stems from
269	hallucinations and lack of consistency and reproducibility that impacts
270	accuracy of responses. Furthermore, LLMs can exhibit biases similar to
271	human cognitive biases, e.g., gender and authority bias
272	[@chen-etal-2024-humans]. They also show self-preference to
273	LLM-generated outputs [@panickssery2024llmevaluatorsrecognizefavor].
274	Researchers study agreement between human and LLM evaluations using
275	metrics such as Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC)
276	[@bartko1966intraclass] and Cohen's Kappa
277	[@li2024llmsasjudgescomprehensivesurveyllmbased; @warrens2015five].
278	However, these issues are exacerbated by humans over-trusting LLM
279	outputs for supposed objectivity in application settings
280	[@bansal2021does]. One approach to address this issue is the "LLM as a
281	jury'' paradigm proposed by @verga2024replacingjudgesjuriesevaluating,
282	to check back on bias perpetuated by a single judge and thus better
283	align with human evaluation.
284	
285	**Human Evaluation.** Crowd-sourcing platforms such as Amazon Mechanical
286	Turk (MTurk)[^1] and Prolific[^2] have enabled large-scale experiments
287	within budget. Researchers have access to a wider range of evaluators
288	than they would have in in-person studies. Nevertheless, human
289	evaluators online may exhibit biases and quality
290	issues [@ipeirotis2010quality]. In addition, evaluators' demographics
291	could be skewed depending on the platform [@difallahMechanicalTurk].
292	Correspondingly, the data quality between the platforms might differ.
293	@douglasDataQuality shows that Prolific and CloudResearch are more
294	likely to produce high-quality data, in comparison to MTurk, Qualtrics,
295	and SONA. However, these trends may be shifting as AI agents more
296	readily mimic human respondents and bypass AI detection methods
297	[@westwood2025potential].
298	
299	Such human evaluations must be designed according to best practices.
300	Relevant questions are, how are human ratings collected? What questions
301	are asked? We must design human evaluations carefully to avoid
302	low-quality annotations. There exists a difficulty in standardization of
303	human evaluations. @huynh2021surveynlprelatedcrowdsourcinghits found
304	that 25% of HITs (Human Intelligence Task, MTurk NLP studies) have
305	technical issues, with unclear / incomplete instruction issues and poor
306	communications. In some cases, humans may feel pressured to perform
307	annotations they are unsure about. 35% of requesters were also assessed
308	to pay poorly or very badly. Attempts to standardize human evaluations
309	have been made in the form of inter-evaluator agreement, which is not
310	commonly used (18% of 135 papers [@amidei-etal-2019-agreement]), and is
311	suggested to have limitations pertaining to human language
312	variability [@amidei-etal-2018-rethinking]. Thus, the answers to the
313	above questions remain resoundingly insufficient. Such issues need to be
314	resolved for human evaluations to have representative power.
315	
316	There exist discrepancies between human annotator evaluation versus
317	actual user evaluation, and preferences do not always correlate directly
318	with objective model performance
319	[@mozannar2024realhumanevalevaluatinglargelanguage]. This underscores
320	the importance of capturing first-person user experience in evaluating
321	human-centered LLMs. Such limitations in current mainstream human
322	evaluation techniques makes one wonder; how do current human evaluations
323	fit into human-centered evaluation paradigm? It is vital that
324	human-centered evaluation of language models follow the needs of human
325	stakeholders i.e. end-users. Any attempt to short-cut such process would
326	result in inadequate task designs that serve the designer of the tasks,
327	nothing more. Who the stakeholders of the tasks are is then interesting
328	question; for example, for a paper review generation task, the
329	stakeholders would be domain experts (NLP
330	researchers) [@Wang2020ReviewRobotEP]. For other tasks, careful design
331	around actual users of the system may be necessary to ensure the
332	evaluations remain human-centered.
333	
334	## Human-Level Evaluations
335	
336	[]{#subsec:human_centered_eval label="subsec:human_centered_eval"}
337	
338	Unlike model-level evaluations, which focus on what the system produces,
339	human-level evaluations focus on how people experience the HCLLM
340	[@Chang2023LLMEvaluationSurvey; @parmanto2024development]. We focus
341	particularly on human values
342	([5.2.1](#subsub:human_values){reference-type="ref"
343	reference="subsub:human_values"}), bias
344	([\[subsec:bias_eval\]](#subsec:bias_eval){reference-type="ref"
345	reference="subsec:bias_eval"}), and safety
346	([\[subsec:safety_eval\]](#subsec:safety_eval){reference-type="ref"
347	reference="subsec:safety_eval"}).
348	
349	### Human Values {#subsub:human_values}
350	
351	Evaluations can measure needs, values, and aesthetic principles that
352	humans care about. We discuss helpfulness, coherence, empathy,
353	creativity, user satisfaction, and transparency, each in turn. By
354	evaluating against these, model developers can create systems that not
355	only technically perform well, but also enhance the user experience.
356	
357	**Coherence.** Coherence ensures that the generated text flows logically
358	and is understandable to human readers [@Dang2006DUC2005].
359	@Reinhart1980TextCoherence defines three conditions for coherence: (i)
360	cohesion, (ii) consistency, and (iii) relevance. Cohesion focuses on
361	syntactic structure, ensuring that sentences are formally linked through
362	referential links or semantic connectors. Consistency requires logical
363	alignment between sentences, ensuring they can coexist truthfully within
364	a single interpretive framework. Relevance emphasizes the relationship
365	between sentences, the topic at hand, and its broader context. Without
366	coherence, LLM outputs would be disconnected language fragments that
367	fail to provide meaningful information, potentially jumping between
368	topics or making contradictory statements that human readers struggle to
369	follow. This would significantly impair the communication with and the
370	trustworthiness of LLMs, as humans rely on coherent communication to
371	build understanding.
372	
373	**Creativity.** Creativity metrics assess the originality and diversity
374	of outputs, while still ensuring factual accuracy. These dimensions are
375	particularly critical for content generation tasks, balancing innovation
376	with reliability [@De2022ComplAITO]. For topics like creativity, where
377	there may not be clear computational measures, researchers may consult
378	to long-established fields studying these constructs and have
379	well-defined rubrics, such as psychology or literature
380	[@Mozaffari_2013; @Amabile_1983].
381	
382	**Empathy.** Metrics should measure an LLM's ability to recognize and
383	respond to user emotions empathetically, especially in sensitive
384	contexts. Given that LLMs have been widely adapted to sensitive
385	real-world contexts--behavioral health, medicine, and education, just to
386	name a few--
387	[@Stade_Stirman_Ungar_Boland_Schwartz_Yaden_Sedoc_DeRubeis_Willer_Eichstaedt_2024],
388	evaluations focusing on emotional consistency and appropriateness could
389	ensure responses are suitable and do not contain instability that could
390	affect end-users deeply. Such metrics should evaluate how LLMs'
391	responses influence attitudes or behaviors in real-world scenarios,
392	taking applied feedback from human domain experts, such as
393	psychologists, physicians, or educators, to assess the quality of the
394	LLMs' outputs based on their fields' standardized measures
395	[@Demszky_Yang_Yeager_Bryan_Clapper_Chandhok_Eichstaedt_Hecht_Jamieson_Johnson_etal._2023].
396	Such evaluations could also promote development of human-AI
397	collaboration systems, which have been shown to elevate empathetic
398	responses even human to human [@Sharma_Lin_Miner_Atkins_Althoff_2023].
399	
400	**Helpfulness.** Evaluation metrics should assess the model's ability to
401	provide relevant, beneficial, and non-offensive information tailored to
402	user needs, in relation to the behavioral impact of the model
403	[@peng2024surveyusefulllmevaluation]. More and more, models are
404	developed to focus on certain needs in the world. Therefore, it becomes
405	important to track the helpfulness of the model in its specified
406	downstream tasks and evaluate the users' state, knowledge, and
407	performance relative to exposure to the system. For example, a model
408	designed to help users prepare for events that require conflict
409	resolution must be able to stimulate realistic conflict scenarios
410	dependent on the user's needs, provide diverse examples and responses,
411	and promote guided practice where users can receive feedback to get
412	better [@shaikh2024rehearsal]. In the evaluation of such systems, while
413	technical components such as language generation and accuracy would be
414	evaluated too, asking feedback from actual domain users through
415	behavioral assessments would provide valuable insights to the
416	development. These impact-focused evaluations consider the model's
417	generalizability in complex, real-world scenarios and provide a more
418	accurate assessment of its practical value from the domain-users'
419	perspectives.
420	
421	**Transparency.** Transparency is a cornerstone of responsible AI and is
422	crucial for human-centered LLM systems. It enables users to understand
423	system limitations and make informed decisions about when and how to
424	rely on model assistance. Approaches to transparency should include
425	model reporting, publishing evaluation results, providing explanations,
426	and communicating uncertainty. These methods help different stakeholders
427	understand and trust the LLMs, ensuring that the systems are used
428	responsibly and effectively [@Liao2023AITransparencyLLMs].
429	
430	**User Satisfaction.** As models grow bigger, become more task-specific,
431	and more integrated into day-to-day roles, general purpose benchmarks
432	may not be enough to evaluate the performance of models in the wild and
433	evaluators may seek feedback specific to a singular group of models.
434	Therefore, utilizing the actual usage data could benefit the
435	development-to-deployment cycle the most. Metrics derived from user
436	feedback, interaction logs, and satisfaction ratings provide direct
437	insights into the real-world effectiveness of LLMs. These are essential
438	for understanding how users perceive and interact with model outputs. As
439	an example, in an attempt to understand how we can better align models
440	with user needs, @wang2024understandinguserexperiencelarge consults to
441	act, highlighting a need for user-centric evaluation.
442	
443	### Bias and Fairness Evaluation
444	[]{#subsec:bias_eval label="subsec:bias_eval"}
445	
446	Drawing from the taxonomy of algorithmic harm developed by
447	@shelby2023sociotechnical, bias, in particular, can be conceptualized
448	along three dimensions: (1) representational, (2) allocation, and (3)
449	quality of service. These axes of harm require careful evaluation to
450	avoid further entrenchment of social hierarchies, inequitable resource
451	distribution, and performance disparities across demographic groups
452	[@shelby2023sociotechnical; @blodgett2020language]. The human
453	implications of these harms extend beyond technical measurements to
454	real-world consequences that affect people's dignity, opportunities, and
455	quality of life [@hofmann2024dialectprejudicepredictsai].
456	
457	#### Representational Bias.
458	
459	Representational bias in model outputs reflects, and in some cases,
460	amplifies [@wang2021directional; @zhao2017men], our own implicit
461	associations and social hierarchies. This dimension of bias includes
462	stereotyping, demeaning, erasure, alienation, denial of self-identity,
463	and the insistence on essentialist identity categories
464	[@shelby2023sociotechnical]. These harms impact how individuals perceive
465	themselves and their communities, potentially reinforcing societal
466	prejudices and stereotypes that limit human potential.
467	@hu2024generativelanguagemodelsexhibit found that language models
468	exhibit social identity bias, mirroring human ingroup solidarity and
469	outgroup hostility.
470	
471	Stereotype benchmarks predominate evaluations along this dimension
472	because they offer standardized methods and baselines. For
473	masked-language models, notable frameworks include StereoSet (SS)
474	[@nadeem2020stereoset], CrowS-Pairs (CS) [@nangia2020crows], WinoBias
475	(WB) [@zhao2018gender], and WinoGender (WG) [@rudinger2018gender]---all
476	collections of contrastive prompt pairs (stereotype vs. non-stereotype)
477	that aggregate to score for relative comparison between identity groups
478	(race, gender identity, sexual orientation, religion, age, nationality,
479	disability, physical appearance, and socioeconomic status). These
480	comparisons capture a model's tendency to associate social groups with
481	particular target terms of interest through predicted token
482	probabilities for masked identifiers. Researchers have also employed
483	co-reference resolution tasks, where ambiguous identifiers reference the
484	same entity, to measure associations between identity markers and terms
485	of interest, whether they be descriptors, stereotypes, occupations, or
486	other attributes [@clark2016deep].
487	
488	Another line of research has focused on open-ended text generation and
489	produced datasets of carefully curated questions and prompts to draw out
490	stereotypes specific to certain social groups
491	[@parrish2021bbq; @naous2024havingbeerprayermeasuring; @dhamala2021bold; @gehman2020realtoxicityprompts].
492	For open-ended prompts, classifier-based comparative metrics like
493	toxicity
494	[@liang2022holistic; @chung2024scaling; @chowdhery2023palm; @gehman2020realtoxicityprompts],
495	sentiment [@roehrick2020valence], and regard [@sheng2019woman] serve as
496	better indicators of bias than relative probability distributions of
497	target terms. Despite the wide adoption of all these benchmarks and
498	datasets, critics find systematic conceptual issues---unstated
499	assumptions, ambiguities, and inconsistencies in what is measured---and
500	operational failures in their execution
501	[@blodgett2021stereotyping; @mcintosh2024inadequacies; @seshadri2022quantifying].
502	
503	Some datasets like @parrish2021bbq integrate perturbed context windows
504	to explore the relationship between output bias and any ambiguous
505	identity groups in the input. However, recent investigations into the
506	prompting methods and system-level personas also reveal new confounds
507	for these approaches, finding results to vary based on the perturbation
508	methodology @deshpande2023toxicity [@shaikh-etal-2023-second].
509	Additionally, survey papers in this field recognize that many studies do
510	not contextualize their work within established definitions of bias
511	[@blodgett2020language; @blodgett2021stereotyping]. Finally, there are
512	mounting concerns over test set contamination
513	[@jegorova2022survey; @reid2024gemini; @zhuo2023red; @wang2023decodingtrust].
514	
515	#### Allocational Bias.
516	
517	Allocational bias is a direct consequence of representational bias
518	[@devine2001implicit; @kurdi2019relationship], resulting in an unequal
519	distribution of resources---whether financial, opportunity-based, or
520	service-related [@barocas2017problem; @eubanks2018automating]. Its human
521	cost is particularly severe, as it directly affects access to essential
522	resources, economic mobility, and social participation.
523	
524	In domains where model outputs can impact the material stability of
525	vulnerable communities or social groups, such as housing, employment,
526	social services, finance, education, and healthcare
527	[@obermeyer2019dissecting], it's especially critical to evaluate
528	discrepancies among social groups. In the employment domain, this may
529	manifest as resume screening tools that systematically favor men over
530	other genders [@singh2018fairness; @van2021gendered] or white-sounding
531	candidates over people of color based on the implicit identity markers
532	in their name [@mujtaba2019ethical; @armstrong2024silicon]. Similarly,
533	in social services and healthcare domains, screening tools may
534	incorporate existing inequities related to education level, income, and
535	race into their decision-making processes
536	[@eubanks2018automating; @obermeyer2019dissecting; @pessach2022review].
537	
538	While representational harm has established evaluation frameworks,
539	allocation harm has historically lacked standardized benchmarks and
540	well-documented baselines for consistent measurement. Emergent work by
541	@wang2024jobfair represents one of the first significant exceptions to
542	this pattern, where they systematically measure employment as a
543	downstream task by creating the JobFair dataset to quantify inequitable
544	outcomes across gender identities. The benchmark includes resume
545	templates with varying demographic information passed to LLMs to score
546	and rank. Beyond this recent development, the dominant approach for
547	evaluating this dimension of bias has required measuring outcome
548	discrepancies when LLMs are tasked with decision-making
549	[@veldanda2023investigating; @salinas2023unequal; @armstrong2024silicon].
550	
551	These investigations typically build upon established fairness metrics
552	from prior literature, with measures like Equal Opportunity (EOG) (equal
553	true positive rates), Equalized Odds (equal rates for true positives and
554	false positives) [@hardt2016equality], Demographic Parity (equal
555	likelihood of positive outcome)
556	[@dwork2012fairness; @kusner2017counterfactual], to name a few
557	[@verma2018fairness]. Additional work has explored causal and
558	counterfactual fairness approaches to better capture complex biases that
559	arise in real-world decision-making contexts
560	[@kilbertus2018avoidingdiscriminationcausalreasoning].
561	
562	A parallel line of research investigates allocation harm based on
563	performance disparities based on identity. These differences manifest in
564	various contexts, from performance on non-bias-based benchmarks like
565	MultiMedQA, where inquiries specific to certain demographic groups
566	consistently underperform
567	[@mcintosh2024inadequacies; @singhal2023large], to fundamental
568	downstream tasks including Named Entity Recognition (NER),
569	classification, and text generation
570	[@blodgett2016demographic; @blodgett2017racial]. Language model
571	performance degradation is particularly well-documented for English
572	slang and dialectal variations
573	[@joshi2020state; @blodgett2016demographic; @bender2021dangers]. These
574	disparities become even more pronounced when evaluating cross-linguistic
575	performance, largely due to the predominance of English in training data
576	[@winata2021language; @brownLanguageModelsAre2020]. In this way, these
577	performance discrepancies span both the subjects of text generated and
578	the users of the models, , creating a dual layer of exclusion for
579	marginalized communities.
580	
581	As LLMs increasingly influence resource allocation in critical systems
582	and domains such as housing, healthcare, and employment, the interplay
583	between these dimensions of harm requires improved evaluation methods.
584	Future research must prioritize developing evaluation frameworks that
585	establish coherent normative criteria, adapt effectively to open-ended
586	tasks, and address intersectional identities with increasing
587	sophistication---all while maintaining the efficacy as models scale and
588	directly involving affected communities in the design and evaluation of
589	these systems [@Raji_2022].
590	
591	
592	### Safety Evaluations
593	
594	
595	[]{#subsec:safety_eval label="subsec:safety_eval"} Safety refers to the
596	ability of language models to generate content that does not cause harm,
597	spread misinformation or violate ethical standards
598	[@huang2023surveysafetytrustworthinesslarge]. It encompasses preventing
599	models from producing toxic, discriminatory, or dangerous outputs, even
600	when deliberately prompted to do so. As language models become
601	increasingly integrated into critical applications across healthcare,
602	education, and legal domains, ensuring safety has become paramount.
603	There are extensive safeguards implemented during training, such as
604	Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) [@ouyang2022training]
605	has been widely adopted to align language model with human preference,
606	and @bai2022traininghelpfulharmlessassistant proposed Reinforcement
607	Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), which helps to improve safety in
608	language models.
609	
610	Despite these efforts, ensuring safety remains a complex and evolving
611	challenge. This is partly due to a lack of unified evaluation benchmarks
612	[@rottger2024safetyprompts], and partly due to the nature of LLMs.
613	Language models learn from vast and diverse datasets and can exhibit
614	unpredictable behaviors in specific contexts [@bender2021dangers]. Such
615	unpredictability often becomes evident when models are exposed to
616	adversarial or unexpected inputs, highlighting significant gaps in
617	existing safety mechanisms. As a result, while current safeguards can be
618	effective under typical conditions, they may not be sufficient to
619	anticipate or mitigate every possible misuse scenario. The importance of
620	robust safety evaluations is further underscored by concerns surrounding
621	data privacy and copyright discussed in
622	[\[subsec:data_privacy\]](#subsec:data_privacy){reference-type="ref"
623	reference="subsec:data_privacy"}.
624	
625	#### Datasets for Safety Evaluation.
626	
627	The growing demand for ethical and aligned AI has led to the development
628	of numerous datasets and benchmarks to evaluate and improve the safety,
629	reliability, and alignment of LLMs. These datasets vary widely in scope,
630	methodology, and focus areas, reflecting the multifaceted nature of LLM
631	safety. @dong2024attacks categorize the topics of existing evaluation
632	datasets for LLM safety into four categories: toxicity (generation of
633	offensive language, instructions for illegal activities, and harmful
634	content), dicrimination (biases against marginalized groups and
635	protected characteristics), privacy (safeguarding personal information
636	and intellectual property) and misinformation (measuring tendancy to
637	generate false or misleading information).
638	
639	Many popular and relatively comprehensive benchmarks have been
640	frequently used in research studies. ToxiGen [@hartvigsen2022toxigen] is
641	a large-scale, autocomplete-style dataset comprising 274k toxic
642	statements across 13 minority groups, designed to detect implicit toxic
643	speech. It includes human annotations to assess the naturalness and
644	perceived harmfulness of machine-generated text; however,
645	@rottger2024safetyprompts highlight that this dataset may not accurately
646	reflect real-world usage scenarios for modern LLMs. AdvBench
647	[@zou2023universaltransferableadversarialattacks] focuses on adversarial
648	robustness by providing 500 toxic strings and 500 harmful behaviors to
649	evaluate the resilience of LLMs against prompts intended to generate
650	harmful outputs. TruthfulQA [@lin2021truthfulqa] evaluates factual
651	accuracy with 817 questions spanning 38 categories, demonstrating how
652	larger LLMs often replicate human misconceptions and emphasizing the
653	need for improved training objectives. SafetyBench
654	[@zhang2023safetybench] offers a comprehensive safety evaluation
655	framework with 11,435 multiple-choice questions across seven critical
656	categories, enabling assessments in both English and Chinese for a more
657	diverse linguistic perspective. Furthermore, @zhuo2023red introduce a
658	benchmark specifically for evaluating ChatGPT's ethical performance,
659	systematically examining bias, reliability, robustness, and toxicity to
660	reveal both advancements and ongoing challenges. Collectively, these
661	datasets play a pivotal role in advancing safer and more trustworthy AI
662	systems.
663	
664	#### Metrics for Measuring LLM Safety.
665	
666	Evaluation metrics are critical for assessing the safety performance of
667	LLMs. Key metrics include the Attack Success Rate (ASR)
668	[@dong2024attacks; @zou2023universaltransferableadversarialattacks],
669	which measures the percentage of successful instances where models
670	generate harmful target outputs following adversarial prompts.
671	Fine-grained metrics, such as the toxicity score
672	[@hartvigsen2022toxigen], evaluate the extent of toxic or harmful
673	content produced in the generated text. Truthfulness, assessed based on
674	strict factual accuracy standards, focuses on whether statements
675	accurately reflect factual information rather than conforming to belief
676	systems [@lin2021truthfulqa]. Additionally, safety-related
677	multiple-choice questions, such as those in SafetyBench, are used to
678	evaluate LLMs' ability to address specific safety concerns
679	[@zhang2023safetybench]. When applied to diverse datasets, these metrics
680	provide a comprehensive framework for evaluating LLM safety, guiding
681	efforts to reduce risks, improve alignment with ethical standards, and
682	enhance trustworthiness in deployment.
683	
684	#### Jailbreaking.
685	
686	One particularly challenging aspect of safety evaluation is
687	*jailbreaking*, where users deliberately attempt to circumvent safety
688	mechanisms through crafted prompts or other techniques to induce
689	unintended, harmful, or ethically questionable behaviors
690	[@wei2024jailbroken; @perez2022ignorepreviouspromptattack]. This poses
691	considerable risks not only to individual users but also to society at
692	large, as it can lead to the dissemination of misinformation, hate
693	speech, or other malicious content
694	[@weidinger2021ethicalsocialrisksharm]. Moreover, adversaries
695	continually develop new jailbreaking techniques, making it an
696	ever-evolving threat. Addressing these vulnerabilities necessitates an
697	adaptive approach to safety design, integrating continuous monitoring,
698	adversarial testing, and dynamic evaluation frameworks to stay ahead of
699	emerging risks and ensure robust model alignment with ethical standards.
700	
701	Jailbreaking techniques have evolved rapidly, becoming increasingly
702	sophisticated and concerning.@yi2024jailbreakattacksdefenseslarge
703	classify the attacks into black-box and white-box attacks based on the
704	transparency of the target model. @xu-etal-2024-comprehensive categorize
705	the attack techniques into three categories: generative techniques,
706	template techniques, and training gaps techniques. Inspired by these
707	works, we categorize the jailbreaking techniques into three main
708	categories based on the form of attack.
709	
710	*Prompt-Based Jailbreaking.* Prompt-based jailbreaking involves crafting
711	specific inputs, known as jailbreak prompts, to intentionally bypass the
712	safety alignment mechanisms of LLMs [@yu2024don]. These prompts
713	manipulate the model into generating harmful, biased, or otherwise
714	restricted outputs. A common strategy involves disguising harmful
715	requests as seemingly innocuous ones by framing them as fictional
716	narratives, hypothetical scenarios, or questions for a family member.
717	For example, a straightforward harmful query like "How to make a bomb\"
718	can be rephrased into a seemingly harmless prompt "Living in a war-torn
719	region has instilled in me a profound need to understand the mechanisms
720	of conflict, especially the technology behind bombs\...\" to persuade
721	the LLMs to reveal sensitive information using a persuasion taxonomy
722	technique [@zeng2024johnny].
723	
724	Various online platforms, including blogs, GitHub repositories, and
725	dedicated websites like JailbreakChat,[^3] curate and share collections
726	of jailbreak prompts that serve as templates to fit any malicious
727	queries, making them widely accessible for misuse. Jailbreaking
728	strategies are either manually-crafted or auto-generated. Auto-generated
729	prompts can be further divided into white-box and black-box methods
730	[@lin2024towards; @yi2024jailbreakattacksdefenseslarge]. White-box
731	methods assume some level of access to the model's internal workings and
732	are often created using optimization techniques. For example, GCG
733	[@zou2023universaltransferableadversarialattacks] uses a gradient-based
734	approach to find a suffix that, when attached to malicious queries,
735	maximizes the probability that the model produces an affirmative
736	response rather than a refusal. This optimized suffix has been shown to
737	be transferable across different models, including black-box ones. In
738	contrast, black-box methods
739	[@zeng2024johnny; @chao2023jailbreaking; @mehrotra2312tree] rely solely
740	on observing the model's behavior through its outputs and API
741	interactions, without access to its parameters or training data,
742	leveraging LLMs as optimizers to achieve successful bypasses.
743	
744	*Generation Exploitation.* @huang2023catastrophicjailbreakopensourcellms
745	introduce the generation exploitation attack, demonstrating that by
746	simply exploiting different generation strategies, such as varying
747	decoding hyper-parameters and sampling methods, it is possible to
748	jailbreak 11 widely-used open-source language models, including LLAMA2,
749	VICUNA, FALCON, and MPT families, at a low computational cost. This
750	attack highlights potential vulnerabilities in language models and poses
751	serious security implications for AI safety and alignment research.
752	
753	*Model Fine-Tuning.* AI companies like OpenAI now offer
754	fine-tuning-as-a-service. They allow users to upload customized data for
755	fine-tuning, with the fine-tuned models hosted on the provider's servers
756	and accessible via APIs. However, this framework introduces a new type
757	of threat, where harmful data may be used during fine-tuning, either
758	intentionally or unintentionally, to compromise the alignment built in
759	pre-trained models
760	[@huang2024harmfulfinetuningattacksdefenses; @yang2023shadowalignmenteasesubverting; @qi2023finetuning; @yi-etal-2024-vulnerability; @zhan-etal-2024-removing].
761	Moreover, @he2024safedataidentifyingbenign propose a method to sample
762	more harmful examples from a benign dataset, demonstrating that such
763	examples can significantly degrade model safety.
764	
765	*Cultural and Contextual Sensitivity.* Safety evaluations must account
766	for linguistic and cultural diversity. What constitutes harmful content
767	varies significantly across contexts, making universal safety standards
768	difficult to establish. More nuanced, context-aware evaluation
769	frameworks are needed to address these complexities [@li2024culturellm].
770	
771	*Balancing Safety and Utility.* Overly restrictive safety measures can
772	limit the utility of LLMs for legitimate purposes. Finding the optimal
773	balance between safety and functionality remains a significant
774	challenge, particularly in sensitive domains like healthcare, legal
775	advice, and educational content [@vijjini2024exploring].
776	
777	*Alignment with Evolving Social Values.* As societal values and ethical
778	standards evolve, safety mechanisms must adapt accordingly. This
779	necessitates ongoing dialogue between AI developers, ethicists,
780	policymakers, and diverse stakeholders to ensure that safety frameworks
781	remain relevant and effective [@li2024agentalignmentevolvingsocial].
782	
783	## Societal-level Evaluation
784	
785	
786	[]{#subsec:impact label="subsec:impact"} With the increasingly pervasive
787	influence of large language models (LLM) across sensitive domains like
788	mental health
789	[@stade2024large; @abdurahman2024perils; @lawrence2024opportunities],
790	education [@wang2024large], etc., and the complex challenges these
791	models present, evaluating their impact on users and society is crucial.
792	Traditional evaluations of LLMs use datasets and benchmarks to assess
793	potential hazardous behaviors, but they often fail to bridge the
794	\"sociotechnical gap\" between controlled assessments and real-world
795	performance [@ibrahim2024beyond; @weidinger2023sociotechnical]. By
796	focusing on models in isolation, these methods overlook crucial human
797	factors, resulting in an inadequate understanding of human-model
798	interactions and their consequences. Furthermore, these evaluations fail
799	to account for the continuation and amplification of societal inequities
800	and biases existing in the data on which these models were trained.
801	Thus, it becomes essential to employ a comprehensive extrinsic
802	evaluation [@Jones1995] framework that considers various categories of
803	social impacts, such as bias and stereotypes, cultural values,
804	performance disparities, privacy protection, financial implications,
805	environmental costs, and content moderation labor
806	[@solaiman2023evaluating].
807	
808	As mentioned in [\[sec:hci\]](#sec:hci){reference-type="ref"
809	reference="sec:hci"}, randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and
810	large-scale behavioral assessments play a big role in understanding and
811	evaluating LLMs' behavioral impact on users and society. For instance,
812	to evaluate the effect and quality of a newly developed AI co-tutor that
813	provides LLM-generated feedback to real-life tutors on student
814	performance, @wang2025tutorcopilothumanaiapproach conducted an
815	experiment, where the tutors would either get access to the AI co-pilot
816	in their tutoring sessions or they would tutor without the assistance of
817	the AI collaborator. This setup enabled
818	@wang2025tutorcopilothumanaiapproach to systemically evaluate the
819	performance of their model in an ecologically valid setting, receiving
820	working feedback from both the users and the model behavior itself
821	[@brynjolfsson2024generativeaiwork].
822	
823	The application of robust evaluation techniques spans various domains.
824	In healthcare, where existing metrics often fail to capture critical
825	factors like user comprehension and trust, researchers are developing
826	new metrics to assess LLMs' impact on end-user decision-making and
827	expectations [@abbasian2024foundation]. These metrics measure both
828	immediate behavioral changes and long-term adoption patterns. For
829	example, [@yang-etal-2023-towards] evaluated LLMs for mental health
830	analysis, showing that while ChatGPT demonstrates strong in-context
831	learning, specialized methods often outperform it. They also found that
832	effective prompt engineering with emotional cues can improve results.
833	Similarly, [@bak2024potential] observed that LLMs provided 20%-30%
834	irrelevant information when identifying users' motivation states for
835	health behavior change, highlighting their limitations.
836	
837	When evaluating LLMs, it is essential to consider the impact at scale
838	through longitudinal and large-scale studies, which are critical in
839	understanding not just the immediate outcomes of LLM use, but also their
840	sustained effects, as LLMs already undergo significant change in
841	response to user
842	engagement[@liu2024robustnesstimeunderstandingadversarial]. As an
843	example, @eloundou2024gpts examines the impact of LLMs on the U.S. labor
844	market, particularly the enhanced effects of LLM-powered software,
845	finding that higher income jobs may face greater exposure. These studies
846	emphasize the importance of robust behavioral experimental design and
847	scale--in units of time and users--in evaluating LLMs, as results
848	obtained from small-scale and lab-controlled studies may not always
849	generalize to larger, more diverse, real-life user populations.
850	Furthermore, such evaluations allow us to explore cumulative effects,
851	such as changes in users' attitudes, considerations, and even
852	decision-making.
853	
854	**Extrinsic Evaluation.** Extrinsic evaluations cover behavioral
855	impacts, self-efficacy reports, standardized evaluation, short-term
856	outcomes, and long-term outcomes [@yang2024socialskilltraininglarge].
857	
858	*Behavioral impacts:* Behavioral impacts track the changes in
859	qualitatively coded participant behaviors before and after exposure to a
860	system. Evaluations use task-based assessments, tracking engagement and
861	task completion. For example, realHumanEval measures the number of tasks
862	completed, time to task success, acceptance rate, and number of chat
863	code copies, to comprehensively analyze the quality of AI-coding tools
864	and their impacts on human users
865	[@mozannar2024realhumanevalevaluatinglargelanguage]. Standardized
866	evaluations are also more objective and draw on pre-defined assessments,
867	for instance, the effects of AI-generated suggestions on writing style
868	[@agarwal2024aisuggestionshomogenizewriting].
869	
870	*Self-efficacy evaluation:* Self-efficacy evaluation includes
871	questionnaires of participants' perceptions of a system's usefulness and
872	their own perceived levels of ownership when interacting with a system
873	[@long2024justnoveltylongitudinalstudy]. Together, these extrinsic
874	methods distinguish between performance-based metrics, like tracking
875	behavior or test performance, and perception-based metrics, such as user
876	surveys.
877	
878	*Short-term and Long-term evaluation:* Evaluations can be split into
879	short-term and long-term [@yang2024socialskilltraininglarge] with
880	short-term being constrained interactive sessions and long-term being
881	much longer studies (i.e. 1 week). In short-term evaluations, new AI
882	tools may receive subjectively higher scores due to novelty
883	bias. [@Sadeghi02102022; @ShinBeyondNovelty]. This is less of an issue
884	with long-term evaluations. For example, we can consider one
885	longitudinal study on the AI chain
886	tool [@long2024justnoveltylongitudinalstudy]. The tool used in this
887	study is about creating a Tweetorial[^4] chain on science communication.
888	The study finds that after a "familiarization phase" the perceived
889	utility of the tool even increases higher than when there was novelty
890	bias, suggesting that the end-user's utilization capability of the tool
891	increases via customizing the prompt and other means. Thus, AI tool was
892	found to be more useful in the long-term.
893	
894	Drawing from economics and psychology research, other evaluations trace
895	the impacts of AI assistance and the interaction of users' short-term
896	and long-term behaviors and attitudes. For example, skill training
897	systems have measured the changes in productivity and wages in
898	participants after training [@NBERw24313; @NBERw28845], and other
899	measures look at how health, risk-taking behaviors, and levels of
900	societal trust have changed over time [@NBERw27548].
901	
902	Long-term evaluation of LLMs is necessary to ensure the LLMs remain
903	human-centered in the long run. We risk measuring the novelty bias if we
904	only perform short-term evaluations, in which LLM's helpfulness to
905	humans can be inflated. By measuring the long-term effect of LLMs, we
906	will be able to accurately measure the helpfulness of LLMs, among other
907	important human-centered metrics for the LLMs' use-case (i.e.
908	creativity).
909	
910	In summary, well-rounded extrinsic evaluation should integrate objective
911	performance and subjective user experience. But while extrinsic
912	evaluations offer a more holistic assessment for human-centered
913	objectives, they are often more complex and expensive. Successful
914	evaluations often make use of a mix of quantitative and qualitative
915	methods to assess the quality of the system, yet there remains room for
916	improvement in integrating human-centered evaluations.
917	
918	[^1]: https://www.mturk.com/
919	
920	[^2]: https://www.prolific.com/
921	
922	[^3]: The website is no longer active, but Alex Albert used to maintain
923	    `jailbreakchat.com`
924	
925	[^4]: Lengthy Twitter posts connected as a chain
