8	---
9	
10	# Responsible Human-Centered LLMs
11	
12	
13	[]{#sec:responsible label="sec:responsible"} In this chapter, we
14	highlight three broad properties that underpin a responsible deployment
15	of HCLLMs, and we explore the tensions and relationships between these
16	ideals (Figure [1](#fig:responsible){reference-type="ref"
17	reference="fig:responsible"}). The first property is ***interpretability
18	([\[subsec:interpretability\]](#subsec:interpretability){reference-type="ref"
19	reference="subsec:interpretability"})***: an HCLLM's input-output
20	transformations should be understood. This property is first, since it
21	complements our next two properties, ***steerability
22	([\[subsec:steerability\]](#subsec:steerability){reference-type="ref"
23	reference="subsec:steerability"})*** and ***safety
24	([6.3](#subsec:safety){reference-type="ref"
25	reference="subsec:safety"})***. Steerable models can be aligned along a
26	pre-selected dimension, and safe models do not produce undesirable
27	outputs. If we have an interpretable model, we may obtain a more
28	steerable model through feature-level control, and we may obtain a safer
29	model by isolating and removing harmful representations.
30	
31	What makes responsible HCLLMs challenging is that these properties are
32	not only complementary, but also in tension. If we make a model more
33	steerable to individual user preferences, this may undermine safety
34	constraints, while overly rigid safety guardrails can limit a model's
35	ability to adapt to legitimate, diverse human needs. And although
36	interpretability supports steerability and safety in many ways, certain
37	alignment and steering methods can make models less interpretable. For
38	example, reward functions used in alignment introduce an additional
39	layer of complexity, and these functions are non-identifiable
40	[@joselowitz2025insights]. Multiple distinct reward functions can yield
41	similar policy behavior. As we discuss each of these three properties,
42	steerability, safety, and interpretability, we will cover current
43	approaches in the literature and then provide directions for future
44	research.
45	
46	![We enumerate three properties for the responsible HCLLM deployment:
47	***interpretability
48	([\[subsec:interpretability\]](#subsec:interpretability){reference-type="ref"
49	reference="subsec:interpretability"})***, ***steerability
50	([\[subsec:steerability\]](#subsec:steerability){reference-type="ref"
51	reference="subsec:steerability"})***, and ***safety
52	([6.3](#subsec:safety){reference-type="ref"
53	reference="subsec:safety"})***. These properties are generally
54	complementary, but tensions between them can make deployment
55	difficult.](../assets/sec6.png){#fig:responsible width="\\linewidth"}
56	
57	## Interpretable and Explainable HCLLMs
58	
59	[]{#subsec:interpretability label="subsec:interpretability"}
60	
61	The first dimension we emphasize is **interpretability and
62	explainability**. Neural networks, as the fundamental building blocks of
63	LLMs, remain largely opaque; the complex interactions between weights
64	and activations make both training dynamics and inference behavior
65	difficult to understand [@8631448]. Yet understanding these systems is
66	critical for ensuring the alignment of LLMs with human values and
67	objectives. We distinguish between two complementary goals:
68	interpretability, which focuses on understanding *how* LLMs operate in
69	general settings; and explainability, which seeks causal explanations
70	for *why* LLMs produce specific behaviors, decisions, or outcomes. Both
71	are essential for human-centered applications, but serve different
72	purposes. Interpretability provides a better understanding of LLM
73	internals, which can help address undesired behaviors such as
74	hallucinations, vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks, and encoded
75	biases. Explainability, by contrast, provides users with comprehensible
76	justification for individual outputs, informing appropriate trust and
77	enabling contestability.
78	
79	### Current Approaches to Interpretability
80	
81	#### Three interconnected areas of modern interpretability research.
82	
83	First, work on understanding internal mechanisms has revealed that
84	transformer components can function as interpretable key-value memories
85	[@geva-etal-2021-transformer] and has begun to uncover how LLMs
86	represent multilingual knowledge
87	[@tang-etal-2024-language; @zhang2024differentstructuralsimilaritiesdifferences].
88	Second, these mechanistic insights have enabled practical interventions
89	on model behavior, such as inference-time steering
90	methods[@li2023inferencetime; @DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2308-10248; @zou2023representationengineeringtopdownapproach; @wu2024reft],
91	while model editing and machine unlearning techniques allow for targeted
92	removal of undesirable traits
93	[@meng2023massediting; @ilharco2023editing; @liu2024rethinkingmachineunlearninglarge].
94	Third, interpretability serves as a diagnostic tool for safety, helping
95	researchers understand jailbreaking vulnerabilities
96	[@arditi2024refusal; @kirch2024featurespromptsjailbreakllms] and
97	identify adversarial attack vectors
98	[@lucki2024adversarialperspectivemachineunlearning; @yu2024robustllmsafeguardingrefusal; @jain2024what].
99	
100	#### Interpretability methods for human-centered purposes.
101	
102	It is important to understand why certain model behaviors arise, such as
103	sycophancy or deception; however, this cannot be done simply by
104	examining model outputs in a post-hoc
105	fashion [@sharma2024towards; @hubinger2024sleeperagentstrainingdeceptive].
106	This shortcoming motivates the need to apply interpretability methods
107	for human-centered purposes. Building on theories such as the linear
108	representation hypothesis [@park2023the], the platonic representation
109	hypothesis [@huh2024position], and universal feature representations
110	across all LLMs [@lan2024sparse], interpretability has been used as a
111	tool to understand different model biases, including social
112	biases [@liu2024devil], cultural biases [@yu2025entangled], and cultural
113	knowledge [@veselovsky2025localized]. Additionally, recent work has
114	sought to identify models' internal representations of important model
115	behaviors, finding that models encode harmfulness and refusal separately
116	[@zhao2025llms] and that three dimensions of sycophancy --- sycophantic
117	agreement, sycophantic praise, and genuine praise --- are all encoded
118	along different linear directions in latent space and can be amplified
119	and suppressed without affecting the other [@vennemeyer2025sycophancy].
120	
121	Another recent application of interpretability on HCLLM can help better
122	model human-AI interactions. In order for LLMs to act as helpful
123	assistants for users, they need to not only understand the user query
124	but develop an understanding of a user's latent traits and needs. A
125	misalignment between a model's representation of the user and a user's
126	true needs can lead to various harmful outcomes, ranging from
127	conversational grounding failures [@shaikh2023grounding] to sycophancy
128	and deception. For example, to make a model's user representation more
129	transparent, @chen2024designing designs a system to extract data related
130	to a user's demographic features and a dashboard that displays this
131	representation. @choi2025scalably similarly extracts latent
132	representations of users in LLMs, and these methods have also been
133	applied to predict the behaviors of personalized LLMs
134	[@karny2025neural].
135	
136	### Current Approaches to Explainability
137	
138	#### Modern explainability research for LLMs pursues several complementary goals.
139	
140	Feature attribution methods identify which inputs most influence
141	outputs, natural language rationales provide human-readable
142	justifications, and counterfactual explanations show how minimal input
143	changes would alter predictions [@10.1145/3639372]. Unlike
144	interpretability, which seeks general understanding of internal
145	mechanisms, explainability focuses on justifying individual predictions
146	in terms that users and stakeholders can act upon. This goal has proven
147	challenging, as traditional explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as LIME
148	and SHAP [@ribeiro2016should] become computationally impractical at the
149	scale of billions of parameters, while LLM-specific approaches such as
150	chain-of-thought reasoning and post-hoc citation generation often
151	prioritize plausibility over faithfulness
152	[@lanham2023measuringfaithfulnesschainofthoughtreasoning; @turpin2023languagemodelsdontsay].
153	For a comprehensive taxonomy of explainability techniques for LLMs, we
154	refer readers to @10.1145/3639372.
155	
156	#### How explainability methods can be used for human-centered purposes.
157	
158	Explainability serves as a foundational element for building user trust
159	and enabling accountability in LLM systems. The ability to assign
160	responsibility for model decisions is essential not only for developing
161	transparent systems but also for supporting downstream regulatory
162	efforts -- for instance, AI in hiring systems, compensation for content
163	creators, and copyright law [@guha2024alignment]. These concerns have
164	motivated legislative action: for instance, the EU AI Act, which became
165	enforceable in 2024, establishes explainability as a legal requirement
166	in critical domains [@euaiact2024].
167	
168	For end users, trust fundamentally depends on calibration (i.e., whether
169	models can reliably express what they know and don't know). Models often
170	struggle to convey uncertainty, both through log-probabilities and
171	linguistic hedging [@zhou2023navigating], although recent work has made
172	progress on both fronts
173	[@tian-etal-2023-just; @li2024fewshotrecalibrationlanguagemodels].
174	Closely related is the problem of citation and attribution. Effective
175	attribution can provide causal explanations for LLM behavior, but
176	current approaches have significant limitations. While RAG systems
177	supply LLMs with relevant context, there is no guarantee that models
178	actually use that context to generate responses
179	[@du-etal-2024-context; @li-etal-2023-large]. Post-hoc citation
180	generation similarly suffers from severe faithfulness issues
181	@liu2023evaluating, motivating work on parametric attribution
182	[@khalifa2024sourceawaretrainingenablesknowledge] and measuring training
183	data influence more broadly
184	[@pmlr-v202-park23c; @grosse2023studyinglargelanguagemodel; @guu2023simfluencemodelinginfluenceindividual].
185	
186	Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning represents a particularly contested
187	approach to explainability. On one hand, CoT outputs provide an
188	accessible window into model reasoning that users can inspect without
189	technical expertise. On the other hand, research has shown that these
190	explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reasons for a
191	model's predictions
192	[@lanham2023measuringfaithfulnesschainofthoughtreasoning; @turpin2023languagemodelsdontsay].
193	This creates a paradox for human-centered design: CoT explanations may
194	increase user trust precisely because they appear plausible, even if
195	they fail to faithfully reflect a model's decision process.
196	
197	Finally, LLMs have shown potential for advancing explainability in other
198	scientific domains. For instance, LLM-powered simulations have enabled
199	HCI designers to explore counterfactual scenarios and reason about
200	design decisions [@park2022social] while LLM-inspired approaches can
201	extract interpretable biological features from protein language models
202	[@simon2024interplm].
203	
204	### Looking Forward
205	
206	#### Providing understanding for model developers.
207	
208	The black-box nature of LLMs, particularly the closed-source ones, makes
209	it difficult to predict and control how models behave. For example, when
210	models provide unsolicited affirmation to the user, it is unclear what
211	*causes* the model to provide that affirmation. As the range of
212	questions and interactions becomes more and more complex and open-ended,
213	interpretability becomes a key tool to answer questions like: how can we
214	determine if a model is personalized? Does the model truly understand a
215	user's intent? Developing an understanding of a model's representation
216	of the user is especially important as people use LLMs for personal
217	questions and even as AI companions. Without an understanding of models'
218	behaviors, model builders risk harming users' well-being
219	[@cheng2025sycophantic].
220	
221	#### Uncovering unintended effects of post-training.
222	
223	Another key application of interpretability for HCLLM is a better
224	understanding of post-training procedures like preference alignment
225	[@ferrao2025anatomy; @movva2025s]. Without more interpretable
226	approaches, post-training can lead to various unintended effects (e.g.
227	sycophancy) that can be difficult to monitor or mitigate post-hoc.
228	Building on existing approaches that refine our understanding of what
229	preference alignment actually optimizes for, model providers can better
230	control and steer behaviors towards desirable directions. For example,
231	representation finetuning and steering
232	[@rimsky2024steering; @wu2025improved; @wu2025axbench; @wu2024reft] have
233	been shown to be a promising way to control an LLM's behaviors, and
234	these methods can be applied to elicit behaviors that are aligned with
235	users' long-term development. The key first step towards making models
236	safer and more steerable towards long-term beneficial objectives would
237	be to understand how they work.
238	
239	## Steerable HCLLMs
240	
241	[]{#subsec:steerability label="subsec:steerability"}
242	
243	### Current Approaches to Steerability
244	
245	**Steerability** is the second dimension we highlight for HCLLM
246	deployment. Steerability is the degree to which a model can be aligned
247	along a particular dimension
248	[@miehling2024evaluatingpromptsteerabilitylarge], such as preferences,
249	norms, or user-constraints [@chen2025steer]. In contrast to static
250	notions of alignment that aim to produce a single globally acceptable
251	behavior, steerability emphasizes conditional control, or the ability to
252	modulate LLM outputs in accord with its particular users. This property
253	is especially important for HCLLMs, which are designed to interact with
254	diverse users embedded in heterogeneous social, cultural, and
255	institutional contexts.
256	
257	Steerability spans multiple dimensions. First, **personalization** is
258	the goal in which an LLM's outputs adaptively reflect the preferences of
259	individual users or groups of users, along with their prior knowledge,
260	goals, and needs [@tseng2024two]. Personalized models should be able to
261	provide more relevant recommendations [@hu2024enhancing], and they
262	should be calibrated to the user's preferred writing styles
263	[@zhang2024personalization], learning styles [@park2024empowering], and
264	norms around privacy [@shao2024privacylens; @asthana2024know] and social
265	behavior [@li2024agentalignmentevolvingsocial]. A user's preferences can
266	be derived from explicit feedback, as in pairwise preference datasets,
267	or from implicit feedback like historical interaction data. For more
268	in-depth discussion of personalization methods, see
269	[\[subsec:personalization\]](#subsec:personalization){reference-type="ref"
270	reference="subsec:personalization"}.
271	
272	Related to personalization is **persona alignment** or role play. Here,
273	the goal is that HCLLMs will adopt consistent identities or roles, like
274	software developers, expert tutors, empathetic counselors, or skeptical
275	reviewers, which remain stable across interactions
276	[@li2024steerability; @samuel2024personagym; @shanahan2023role]. Persona
277	alignment is especially important in multi-agent settings where multiple
278	LLM personas interact and collaborate
279	[@park2023generative; @guo2024large].
280	
281	In addition to better personalization and role playing, steerable HCLLMs
282	should be able to adaptively understand low-resource languages,
283	dialects, or sociolinguistic varieties [@ziems2023multi]. We refer to
284	this target as **linguistic alignment**. This form of steerability is
285	critical for equitable access, as models trained predominantly on
286	high-resource, standardized corpora often underperform for marginalized
287	linguistic communities (see
288	[\[subsec:data_representation\]](#subsec:data_representation){reference-type="ref"
289	reference="subsec:data_representation"}). Finally, **cultural
290	alignment** means that models can be steered to reflect the norms,
291	values, and narratives of particular communities or demographic groups
292	[@santurkar2023opinionslanguagemodelsreflect]. Unlike personalization,
293	which targets individuals, cultural alignment operates at the level of
294	shared practices and collective meaning-making.
295	
296	A range of technical mechanisms support steerability. At inference time,
297	models may be steered through in-context learning, prompt engineering,
298	or output filtering [@wies2023learnability]. Post-hoc control methods
299	can condition generation on specific attributes or enforce constraints
300	via decoding strategies. More structurally, personalized reward models
301	and fine-tuning procedures can encode user- or group-specific objectives
302	into model parameters [@chen2024pal].
303	
304	Steerability is still fundamentally constrained by the representational
305	biases embedded in pre-training and post-training data
306	[@mihalcea2025ai]. If certain identities, linguistic forms, or cultural
307	narratives are underrepresented or stereotyped in the training corpus,
308	then prompt-based steering may have limited expressive range. In this
309	sense, steerability is not just a matter of control at inference time,
310	but is rooted much earlier in data provenance
311	([\[subsec:data_provenance\]](#subsec:data_provenance){reference-type="ref"
312	reference="subsec:data_provenance"}) and evaluation
313	([\[sec:evaluation\]](#sec:evaluation){reference-type="ref"
314	reference="sec:evaluation"}). Steerability starts with measuring where
315	biases arise, localizing their sources in the data pipeline, and
316	redesigning collection and annotation practices accordingly.
317	
318	### Looking Forward
319	
320	Looking forward, we envision several research directions that extend
321	current notions of steerability. First, we consider continual learning
322	for preference, culture, and pluralistic alignment. Continual preference
323	learning would allow models to adapt dynamically to evolving user needs
324	by tracking implicit cues in interaction patterns or contextual data
325	[@shaikh2025gum]. Such systems often rely on persistent memory stores
326	like chat histories or retrieval-augmented generation. A central
327	challenge is achieving this adaptivity while preserving user autonomy
328	and privacy [@zhang2025autonomy]. In cultural and pluralistic alignment,
329	rather than optimizing toward a static representation of *culture* or
330	*user values*, HCLLMs should accommodate evolving norms and intra-group
331	disagreement, as supported by continual learning. One way to elicit
332	these evolving norms is to facilitate community-centered discussion and
333	debate, following methods like STELA [@bergman2024stela]. Rather than
334	treating communities as homogeneous preference aggregates, pluralistic
335	alignment frameworks should model disagreement as a first-class signal.
336	
337	Pluralistic alignment comes with an array of technical and political
338	challenges that will need to be addressed. On the technical side,
339	post-training can induce mode-collapse, in which heterogeneous group
340	preferences and opinions are compressed in a lossy manner, suppressing
341	minority viewpoints and preserving only the majority preferences for a
342	given group
343	[@bisbee2024synthetic; @durmus2024towards; @rottger2024political]. To
344	elicit diverse generations from LLMs, some inference time methods use
345	iterative prompting [@hayati-etal-2024-far; @feng-etal-2024-modular],
346	but these methods are not calibrated to real-world distributions. Other
347	methods involve modifying the prompt with explicit identity terms for
348	diverse user groups [@Giulianelli2023WhatCN], but identity coded names
349	induce models to draw on distributions of stereotypical representations
350	or out-group perceptions rather than in-group perspectives
351	[@wang2025large]. To address mode-collapse in a manner that preserves
352	in-group perspectives, it may be necessary to update LLM priors
353	implicitly through distributionally-aligned in-context examples,
354	following methods like spectrum tuning [@sorensen2025spectrum].
355	
356	It is not only a methodological challenge, but also a political
357	challenge to achieve localized, domain-specific alignment processes that
358	enable communities and stakeholders to meaningfully shape model behavior
359	[@delgado2023participatory]. Methodologically, we have the participatory
360	HCI approaches covered in
361	[\[subsub:participatory\]](#subsub:participatory){reference-type="ref"
362	reference="subsub:participatory"}. However, politically, most model
363	developers lack incentives to share control with communities
364	[@gabriel2020artificial]. Current alignment pipelines are centralized by
365	the small set of companies with resources to develop LLMs. Similarly,
366	academic institutions and governments can serve to centralize
367	decision-making across the LLM development pipeline
368	[@suresh2024participation]. There are a number of less centralized
369	alternatives. For example, Masakhane [@orife2020masakhane] is a network
370	of NLP researchers working on NLP for local African languages, with
371	community involvement at every stage, from dataset creation and
372	annotation to model training. EleutherAI is a distributed,
373	volunteer-driven research collective that has created open pre-training
374	corpora [@gao2020pile800gbdatasetdiverse], models [@black2022gpt], and
375	scaling checkpoints [@biderman2023pythia]. BigScience was a research
376	effort in which over 1,000 researchers from academia and industry
377	coordinated through HuggingFace and built BLOOM [@workshop2022bloom], a
378	176B-parameter multilingual autoregressive language model, with
379	decision-making steps clearly and publicly documented.
380	
381	These initiatives illustrate that steerability does not need to be
382	confined to top-down fine-tuning interfaces or proprietary alignment
383	pipelines. Distributed model development allows communities to steer
384	models from the ground up, establishing linguistic resources, value
385	functions, and development practices that ultimately shape downstream
386	behavior. At the same time, decentralization introduces its own
387	tensions, including coordination costs, uneven resource distribution,
388	and challenges of accountability. Open and community-led efforts may
389	broaden participation, but they must still grapple with questions of
390	safety, quality control, and transparent maintenance of HCLLMs. In the
391	following sections, we will discuss safety
392	([6.3](#subsec:safety){reference-type="ref" reference="subsec:safety"})
393	and interpretability
394	([\[subsec:interpretability\]](#subsec:interpretability){reference-type="ref"
395	reference="subsec:interpretability"}), as well as the tensions between
396	these objectives.
397	
398	## Safe HCLLMs {#subsec:safety}
399	
400	The third dimension we emphasize when building responsible HCLLMs is
401	**safety**. As defined in
402	[\[subsec:safety_eval\]](#subsec:safety_eval){reference-type="ref"
403	reference="subsec:safety_eval"}, safety is conceptualized as preventing
404	LLMs from producing undesirable outputs (i.e., those that may be toxic,
405	harmful, discriminatory, or dangerous), even when prompted to do so. For
406	example, the widespread use of LLMs raises critical concerns about
407	ethical and social risks related to their outputs, including
408	discrimination, hate speech, exclusion, misinformation harms, malicious
409	uses, and so on [@Zhang2022OPTOP; @bender2021dangers]. At the same time,
410	there are concerns that LLMs can be used as agents of harm, such as
411	using AI-generated propaganda for misinformation
412	purposes [@goldstein2024persuasive] or spreading information that can
413	facilitate harmful actions like the manufacturing of
414	weapons [@shaikh-etal-2023-second].
415	
416	We begin by discussing the existing methods that are employed for
417	addressing safety concerns both at the model training and interaction
418	layers. Looking forward, we advocate for expanding beyond this current
419	definition of safety, which focuses on preventing harms, to encompass
420	how we can build HCLLMs that also maximize user benefits.
421	
422	### Current Approaches to Safety
423	
424	First, we will discuss current methods for measuring and mitigating
425	safety concerns. *Red-teaming* is a common practice for identifying
426	harmful behavior through adversarial testing prior to deployment.
427	Red-teaming approaches differ across model providers, and details are
428	often not publicly disclosed as these practices are conducted in
429	industry settings [@feffer2024red]. As @feffer2024red survey,
430	red-teamers typically come from three pools: subject-matter
431	experts [@ahmad2025openai], crowdworkers [@ganguli2022red], or automated
432	methods, such as the language models
433	themselves [@ganguli2022red; @perez2022red]. The objectives for
434	red-teaming can range from broad mandates to identify any harmful
435	behavior to targeted assessments of specific risks, such as those
436	related to national security. After deployment, model providers may also
437	run bug bounty programs that offer incentives for discovering safety or
438	security
439	vulnerabilities [@openai2025_gpt5_bio_bug_bounty; @anthropic2025_model_safety_bug_bounty].
440	In addition to red-teaming efforts, model developers make use of
441	benchmarks and other safety evaluations, which we discuss in detail in
442	[\[subsec:safety_eval\]](#subsec:safety_eval){reference-type="ref"
443	reference="subsec:safety_eval"}.
444	
445	Mitigations can appear at various stages of the model development
446	pipeline. At the pre-training phase, there is interest in filtering
447	datasets to remove toxic content as a preventative
448	safeguard [@obrien2025deepignorance; @mendu2025towards; @stranisci2025they].
449	At the same time, other work has argued that filtering toxic data during
450	pre-training can have detrimental downstream effects, and that including
451	such data at pre-training can actually make these behaviors easier to
452	remove through
453	fine-tuning [@li2025bad; @maini2025safety; @longpre-etal-2024-pretrainers].
454	Many efforts also address safety concerns during post-training.
455	Foundational techniques for modern LLMs, such as RLHF, are useful not
456	only for increasing model helpfulness but also for aligning models to be
457	more harmless [@ouyang2022training]. Building on these principles,
458	additional post-training methods can help automate parts of this
459	process. For instance, Constitutional AI allows researchers to
460	pre-determine a set of ethical principles for the model to adhere
461	to [@bai2022constitutional]. Instruction-tuning methods can also reduce
462	toxicity (see
463	[\[subsubsec:succeses_instruction_tuning\]](#subsubsec:succeses_instruction_tuning){reference-type="ref"
464	reference="subsubsec:succeses_instruction_tuning"}). Once deployed,
465	guardrail models are used to help moderate both user inputs and
466	generated outputs [@inan2023llama; @dong2024building; @rebedea2023nemo].
467	
468	### Looking Forward
469	
470	Like other human-centered objectives, *safety* can be an underspecified,
471	ambiguous, or contested target. As we anticipate the development of more
472	human-centered LLMs, we should be asking whose definitions of safety are
473	prioritized, and how we can design models that not only prevent harm but
474	can actively promote user flourishing.
475	
476	#### Paying heed to long-term harms.
477	
478	As surveyed above, existing AI safety research tends to focus on
479	immediate harms that users face when interacting with models, such as
480	exposure to toxic speech or the production of misinformation. Of course,
481	these harms carry long-term societal consequences. However, an
482	underexplored class of safety problems involves behavior that appears
483	innocuous in the short term but can compound over repeated usage to
484	become problematic. The recent work in this vein has identified specific
485	model properties, such as sycophancy, which can affect users'
486	psychological states and behaviors [@cheng2025sycophantic]. An open
487	challenge lies in measuring these long-term interaction harms, as they
488	are difficult to capture with standard evaluation practices like
489	benchmarking. One alternative approach, as discussed in
490	[\[sec:hci\]](#sec:hci){reference-type="ref" reference="sec:hci"}, can
491	be to run controlled experiments to understand the effect of model
492	properties on users [@cheng2025sycophantic; @kirk2025neural] or to
493	conduct qualitative inquiry [@mathur2025sometimes]. However, this
494	process can be time-intensive and furthermore potentially exposes
495	participants to the very harms being studied. This concern raises the
496	question of what alternative valid methods exist, such as those that can
497	simulate these harms in silica. Beyond measurement, mitigations also
498	remain largely underexplored --- both in terms of interventions at the
499	model design and user interaction paradigms. Researchers have identified
500	properties that can exacerbate harms (e.g., steering models towards
501	being relationship-seeking in model design [@kirk2025neural], sending
502	emotionally laden messages as users try to exit a
503	platform [@de2025emotional]), but translating these insights into
504	preventative measures remains an important and open area for
505	exploration.
506	
507	#### Expanding the definition of safety.
508	
509	A second area of exploration involves expanding *whose* definition of
510	safety is prioritized. Definitions of safety vary considerably across
511	demographic groups, along factors such as ethnicity, age, and
512	gender [@rastogi2025whose; @ali2025operationalizing; @movva2024annotation; @gabriel2020artificial; @aroyo2023dices].
513	These variances are then encoded into models through alignment
514	processes, significantly changing model
515	behavior [@ali2025operationalizing]. Thus, instead of assuming a generic
516	definition of safety, there is interest in better capturing and modeling
517	the diversity of conceptualizations that exist. This direction presents
518	a natural continuation of the existing focus on pluralistic alignment
519	within human-centered LLM research. How do we capture these differing
520	definitions of safety? Some work has tackled the issue through
521	recruiting diverse sets of annotators to rate safety
522	perceptions [@rastogi2025whose; @aroyo2023dices]. Others advocate for
523	engaging with communities in a more participatory fashion to elicit
524	safety goals, which offer a richer understanding of how different
525	communities understand the potential harms of these
526	technologies [@qadri2025case; @bergman2024stela].
527	
528	Despite the benefits of moving away from this "view from nowhere"
529	conception of safety, it is important to remember that communities
530	themselves are not monolithic. Disagreements inevitably arise about what
531	constitutes safe or harmful content or what model behaviors are deemed
532	desired or unacceptable [@gordon2022jury; @gordon2021disagreement].
533	There is a legitimate concern that implementing democratic methods could
534	inadvertently drown out the voices of minority groups. Yet this is not
535	grounds to dismiss democratic or participatory methods for AI safety as
536	a lost cause. As @zimmermanndon outline in their work, there are viable
537	paths forward for reconciling these tensions by drawing on practices
538	from political philosophy. As we move towards a more pluralistic
539	definition of safety, this requires thinking normatively about the
540	contexts in which we jointly maximize or balance considerations across
541	groups of people, recognizing that collective decisions may at times
542	conflict with individual desires or goals.
543	
544	#### Considering not only harms but also benefits.
545	
546	Finally, much of the discussion so far has focused on mitigating harmful
547	behaviors. However, we emphasize that avoiding harm is not the same as
548	maximizing user benefits. In pursuit of human-centered LLMs, we must
549	also prioritize building models that bring positive change for users.
550	This raises important questions about what beneficial model behavior
551	looks like, and whether our current conceptions of safety align with
552	what is truly beneficial. First, we must challenge the assumption that
553	"safe" models are necessarily the best for promoting benefits. As
554	@cai2024antagonistic challenge, perhaps there is a need to design
555	*antagonistic AI* systems that are "actively dismissive, disagreeable,
556	closed-off, critical, flippant, difficult, interrupting." Much like, for
557	instance, a student may be challenged by their teacher in the learning
558	process, when we design for benefits rather than merely minimizing
559	harms, the desired model behavior changes.
560	
561	A second provocation concerns the scope of benefit: rather than thinking
562	only about the one-to-one benefit of a model on an individual user, what
563	about one-to-many benefits? We can envision designing models for
564	collective or group-level good --- for example, models deployed to
565	promote democratic health by finding common ground through
566	deliberation [@tessler2024ai], or models designed to benefit teams by
567	serving as collaborators within group settings. Just as there are
568	differing definitions of what safety means, there are similarly diverse
569	conceptions of benefit, raising parallel questions about whose
570	definition should be prioritized and how we reconcile conflicting views
571	of what constitutes a beneficial outcome.
572

# Responsible Human-Centered LLMs


[]{#sec:responsible label="sec:responsible"} In this chapter, we
highlight three broad properties that underpin a responsible deployment
of HCLLMs, and we explore the tensions and relationships between these
ideals (Figure [1](#fig:responsible){reference-type="ref"
reference="fig:responsible"}). The first property is ***interpretability
([\[subsec:interpretability\]](#subsec:interpretability){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:interpretability"})***: an HCLLM's input-output
transformations should be understood. This property is first, since it
complements our next two properties, ***steerability
([\[subsec:steerability\]](#subsec:steerability){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:steerability"})*** and ***safety
([6.3](#subsec:safety){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:safety"})***. Steerable models can be aligned along a
pre-selected dimension, and safe models do not produce undesirable
outputs. If we have an interpretable model, we may obtain a more
steerable model through feature-level control, and we may obtain a safer
model by isolating and removing harmful representations.

What makes responsible HCLLMs challenging is that these properties are
not only complementary, but also in tension. If we make a model more
steerable to individual user preferences, this may undermine safety
constraints, while overly rigid safety guardrails can limit a model's
ability to adapt to legitimate, diverse human needs. And although
interpretability supports steerability and safety in many ways, certain
alignment and steering methods can make models less interpretable. For
example, reward functions used in alignment introduce an additional
layer of complexity, and these functions are non-identifiable
[@joselowitz2025insights]. Multiple distinct reward functions can yield
similar policy behavior. As we discuss each of these three properties,
steerability, safety, and interpretability, we will cover current
approaches in the literature and then provide directions for future
research.

![We enumerate three properties for the responsible HCLLM deployment:
***interpretability
([\[subsec:interpretability\]](#subsec:interpretability){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:interpretability"})***, ***steerability
([\[subsec:steerability\]](#subsec:steerability){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:steerability"})***, and ***safety
([6.3](#subsec:safety){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:safety"})***. These properties are generally
complementary, but tensions between them can make deployment
difficult.](../assets/sec6.png){#fig:responsible width="\\linewidth"}

## Interpretable and Explainable HCLLMs

[]{#subsec:interpretability label="subsec:interpretability"}

The first dimension we emphasize is **interpretability and
explainability**. Neural networks, as the fundamental building blocks of
LLMs, remain largely opaque; the complex interactions between weights
and activations make both training dynamics and inference behavior
difficult to understand [@8631448]. Yet understanding these systems is
critical for ensuring the alignment of LLMs with human values and
objectives. We distinguish between two complementary goals:
interpretability, which focuses on understanding *how* LLMs operate in
general settings; and explainability, which seeks causal explanations
for *why* LLMs produce specific behaviors, decisions, or outcomes. Both
are essential for human-centered applications, but serve different
purposes. Interpretability provides a better understanding of LLM
internals, which can help address undesired behaviors such as
hallucinations, vulnerabilities to adversarial attacks, and encoded
biases. Explainability, by contrast, provides users with comprehensible
justification for individual outputs, informing appropriate trust and
enabling contestability.

### Current Approaches to Interpretability

#### Three interconnected areas of modern interpretability research.

First, work on understanding internal mechanisms has revealed that
transformer components can function as interpretable key-value memories
[@geva-etal-2021-transformer] and has begun to uncover how LLMs
represent multilingual knowledge
[@tang-etal-2024-language; @zhang2024differentstructuralsimilaritiesdifferences].
Second, these mechanistic insights have enabled practical interventions
on model behavior, such as inference-time steering
methods[@li2023inferencetime; @DBLP:journals/corr/abs-2308-10248; @zou2023representationengineeringtopdownapproach; @wu2024reft],
while model editing and machine unlearning techniques allow for targeted
removal of undesirable traits
[@meng2023massediting; @ilharco2023editing; @liu2024rethinkingmachineunlearninglarge].
Third, interpretability serves as a diagnostic tool for safety, helping
researchers understand jailbreaking vulnerabilities
[@arditi2024refusal; @kirch2024featurespromptsjailbreakllms] and
identify adversarial attack vectors
[@lucki2024adversarialperspectivemachineunlearning; @yu2024robustllmsafeguardingrefusal; @jain2024what].

#### Interpretability methods for human-centered purposes.

It is important to understand why certain model behaviors arise, such as
sycophancy or deception; however, this cannot be done simply by
examining model outputs in a post-hoc
fashion [@sharma2024towards; @hubinger2024sleeperagentstrainingdeceptive].
This shortcoming motivates the need to apply interpretability methods
for human-centered purposes. Building on theories such as the linear
representation hypothesis [@park2023the], the platonic representation
hypothesis [@huh2024position], and universal feature representations
across all LLMs [@lan2024sparse], interpretability has been used as a
tool to understand different model biases, including social
biases [@liu2024devil], cultural biases [@yu2025entangled], and cultural
knowledge [@veselovsky2025localized]. Additionally, recent work has
sought to identify models' internal representations of important model
behaviors, finding that models encode harmfulness and refusal separately
[@zhao2025llms] and that three dimensions of sycophancy --- sycophantic
agreement, sycophantic praise, and genuine praise --- are all encoded
along different linear directions in latent space and can be amplified
and suppressed without affecting the other [@vennemeyer2025sycophancy].

Another recent application of interpretability on HCLLM can help better
model human-AI interactions. In order for LLMs to act as helpful
assistants for users, they need to not only understand the user query
but develop an understanding of a user's latent traits and needs. A
misalignment between a model's representation of the user and a user's
true needs can lead to various harmful outcomes, ranging from
conversational grounding failures [@shaikh2023grounding] to sycophancy
and deception. For example, to make a model's user representation more
transparent, @chen2024designing designs a system to extract data related
to a user's demographic features and a dashboard that displays this
representation. @choi2025scalably similarly extracts latent
representations of users in LLMs, and these methods have also been
applied to predict the behaviors of personalized LLMs
[@karny2025neural].

### Current Approaches to Explainability

#### Modern explainability research for LLMs pursues several complementary goals.

Feature attribution methods identify which inputs most influence
outputs, natural language rationales provide human-readable
justifications, and counterfactual explanations show how minimal input
changes would alter predictions [@10.1145/3639372]. Unlike
interpretability, which seeks general understanding of internal
mechanisms, explainability focuses on justifying individual predictions
in terms that users and stakeholders can act upon. This goal has proven
challenging, as traditional explainable AI (XAI) techniques such as LIME
and SHAP [@ribeiro2016should] become computationally impractical at the
scale of billions of parameters, while LLM-specific approaches such as
chain-of-thought reasoning and post-hoc citation generation often
prioritize plausibility over faithfulness
[@lanham2023measuringfaithfulnesschainofthoughtreasoning; @turpin2023languagemodelsdontsay].
For a comprehensive taxonomy of explainability techniques for LLMs, we
refer readers to @10.1145/3639372.

#### How explainability methods can be used for human-centered purposes.

Explainability serves as a foundational element for building user trust
and enabling accountability in LLM systems. The ability to assign
responsibility for model decisions is essential not only for developing
transparent systems but also for supporting downstream regulatory
efforts -- for instance, AI in hiring systems, compensation for content
creators, and copyright law [@guha2024alignment]. These concerns have
motivated legislative action: for instance, the EU AI Act, which became
enforceable in 2024, establishes explainability as a legal requirement
in critical domains [@euaiact2024].

For end users, trust fundamentally depends on calibration (i.e., whether
models can reliably express what they know and don't know). Models often
struggle to convey uncertainty, both through log-probabilities and
linguistic hedging [@zhou2023navigating], although recent work has made
progress on both fronts
[@tian-etal-2023-just; @li2024fewshotrecalibrationlanguagemodels].
Closely related is the problem of citation and attribution. Effective
attribution can provide causal explanations for LLM behavior, but
current approaches have significant limitations. While RAG systems
supply LLMs with relevant context, there is no guarantee that models
actually use that context to generate responses
[@du-etal-2024-context; @li-etal-2023-large]. Post-hoc citation
generation similarly suffers from severe faithfulness issues
@liu2023evaluating, motivating work on parametric attribution
[@khalifa2024sourceawaretrainingenablesknowledge] and measuring training
data influence more broadly
[@pmlr-v202-park23c; @grosse2023studyinglargelanguagemodel; @guu2023simfluencemodelinginfluenceindividual].

Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning represents a particularly contested
approach to explainability. On one hand, CoT outputs provide an
accessible window into model reasoning that users can inspect without
technical expertise. On the other hand, research has shown that these
explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reasons for a
model's predictions
[@lanham2023measuringfaithfulnesschainofthoughtreasoning; @turpin2023languagemodelsdontsay].
This creates a paradox for human-centered design: CoT explanations may
increase user trust precisely because they appear plausible, even if
they fail to faithfully reflect a model's decision process.

Finally, LLMs have shown potential for advancing explainability in other
scientific domains. For instance, LLM-powered simulations have enabled
HCI designers to explore counterfactual scenarios and reason about
design decisions [@park2022social] while LLM-inspired approaches can
extract interpretable biological features from protein language models
[@simon2024interplm].

### Looking Forward

#### Providing understanding for model developers.

The black-box nature of LLMs, particularly the closed-source ones, makes
it difficult to predict and control how models behave. For example, when
models provide unsolicited affirmation to the user, it is unclear what
*causes* the model to provide that affirmation. As the range of
questions and interactions becomes more and more complex and open-ended,
interpretability becomes a key tool to answer questions like: how can we
determine if a model is personalized? Does the model truly understand a
user's intent? Developing an understanding of a model's representation
of the user is especially important as people use LLMs for personal
questions and even as AI companions. Without an understanding of models'
behaviors, model builders risk harming users' well-being
[@cheng2025sycophantic].

#### Uncovering unintended effects of post-training.

Another key application of interpretability for HCLLM is a better
understanding of post-training procedures like preference alignment
[@ferrao2025anatomy; @movva2025s]. Without more interpretable
approaches, post-training can lead to various unintended effects (e.g.
sycophancy) that can be difficult to monitor or mitigate post-hoc.
Building on existing approaches that refine our understanding of what
preference alignment actually optimizes for, model providers can better
control and steer behaviors towards desirable directions. For example,
representation finetuning and steering
[@rimsky2024steering; @wu2025improved; @wu2025axbench; @wu2024reft] have
been shown to be a promising way to control an LLM's behaviors, and
these methods can be applied to elicit behaviors that are aligned with
users' long-term development. The key first step towards making models
safer and more steerable towards long-term beneficial objectives would
be to understand how they work.

## Steerable HCLLMs

[]{#subsec:steerability label="subsec:steerability"}

### Current Approaches to Steerability

**Steerability** is the second dimension we highlight for HCLLM
deployment. Steerability is the degree to which a model can be aligned
along a particular dimension
[@miehling2024evaluatingpromptsteerabilitylarge], such as preferences,
norms, or user-constraints [@chen2025steer]. In contrast to static
notions of alignment that aim to produce a single globally acceptable
behavior, steerability emphasizes conditional control, or the ability to
modulate LLM outputs in accord with its particular users. This property
is especially important for HCLLMs, which are designed to interact with
diverse users embedded in heterogeneous social, cultural, and
institutional contexts.

Steerability spans multiple dimensions. First, **personalization** is
the goal in which an LLM's outputs adaptively reflect the preferences of
individual users or groups of users, along with their prior knowledge,
goals, and needs [@tseng2024two]. Personalized models should be able to
provide more relevant recommendations [@hu2024enhancing], and they
should be calibrated to the user's preferred writing styles
[@zhang2024personalization], learning styles [@park2024empowering], and
norms around privacy [@shao2024privacylens; @asthana2024know] and social
behavior [@li2024agentalignmentevolvingsocial]. A user's preferences can
be derived from explicit feedback, as in pairwise preference datasets,
or from implicit feedback like historical interaction data. For more
in-depth discussion of personalization methods, see
[\[subsec:personalization\]](#subsec:personalization){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:personalization"}.

Related to personalization is **persona alignment** or role play. Here,
the goal is that HCLLMs will adopt consistent identities or roles, like
software developers, expert tutors, empathetic counselors, or skeptical
reviewers, which remain stable across interactions
[@li2024steerability; @samuel2024personagym; @shanahan2023role]. Persona
alignment is especially important in multi-agent settings where multiple
LLM personas interact and collaborate
[@park2023generative; @guo2024large].

In addition to better personalization and role playing, steerable HCLLMs
should be able to adaptively understand low-resource languages,
dialects, or sociolinguistic varieties [@ziems2023multi]. We refer to
this target as **linguistic alignment**. This form of steerability is
critical for equitable access, as models trained predominantly on
high-resource, standardized corpora often underperform for marginalized
linguistic communities (see
[\[subsec:data_representation\]](#subsec:data_representation){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:data_representation"}). Finally, **cultural
alignment** means that models can be steered to reflect the norms,
values, and narratives of particular communities or demographic groups
[@santurkar2023opinionslanguagemodelsreflect]. Unlike personalization,
which targets individuals, cultural alignment operates at the level of
shared practices and collective meaning-making.

A range of technical mechanisms support steerability. At inference time,
models may be steered through in-context learning, prompt engineering,
or output filtering [@wies2023learnability]. Post-hoc control methods
can condition generation on specific attributes or enforce constraints
via decoding strategies. More structurally, personalized reward models
and fine-tuning procedures can encode user- or group-specific objectives
into model parameters [@chen2024pal].

Steerability is still fundamentally constrained by the representational
biases embedded in pre-training and post-training data
[@mihalcea2025ai]. If certain identities, linguistic forms, or cultural
narratives are underrepresented or stereotyped in the training corpus,
then prompt-based steering may have limited expressive range. In this
sense, steerability is not just a matter of control at inference time,
but is rooted much earlier in data provenance
([\[subsec:data_provenance\]](#subsec:data_provenance){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:data_provenance"}) and evaluation
([\[sec:evaluation\]](#sec:evaluation){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:evaluation"}). Steerability starts with measuring where
biases arise, localizing their sources in the data pipeline, and
redesigning collection and annotation practices accordingly.

### Looking Forward

Looking forward, we envision several research directions that extend
current notions of steerability. First, we consider continual learning
for preference, culture, and pluralistic alignment. Continual preference
learning would allow models to adapt dynamically to evolving user needs
by tracking implicit cues in interaction patterns or contextual data
[@shaikh2025gum]. Such systems often rely on persistent memory stores
like chat histories or retrieval-augmented generation. A central
challenge is achieving this adaptivity while preserving user autonomy
and privacy [@zhang2025autonomy]. In cultural and pluralistic alignment,
rather than optimizing toward a static representation of *culture* or
*user values*, HCLLMs should accommodate evolving norms and intra-group
disagreement, as supported by continual learning. One way to elicit
these evolving norms is to facilitate community-centered discussion and
debate, following methods like STELA [@bergman2024stela]. Rather than
treating communities as homogeneous preference aggregates, pluralistic
alignment frameworks should model disagreement as a first-class signal.

Pluralistic alignment comes with an array of technical and political
challenges that will need to be addressed. On the technical side,
post-training can induce mode-collapse, in which heterogeneous group
preferences and opinions are compressed in a lossy manner, suppressing
minority viewpoints and preserving only the majority preferences for a
given group
[@bisbee2024synthetic; @durmus2024towards; @rottger2024political]. To
elicit diverse generations from LLMs, some inference time methods use
iterative prompting [@hayati-etal-2024-far; @feng-etal-2024-modular],
but these methods are not calibrated to real-world distributions. Other
methods involve modifying the prompt with explicit identity terms for
diverse user groups [@Giulianelli2023WhatCN], but identity coded names
induce models to draw on distributions of stereotypical representations
or out-group perceptions rather than in-group perspectives
[@wang2025large]. To address mode-collapse in a manner that preserves
in-group perspectives, it may be necessary to update LLM priors
implicitly through distributionally-aligned in-context examples,
following methods like spectrum tuning [@sorensen2025spectrum].

It is not only a methodological challenge, but also a political
challenge to achieve localized, domain-specific alignment processes that
enable communities and stakeholders to meaningfully shape model behavior
[@delgado2023participatory]. Methodologically, we have the participatory
HCI approaches covered in
[\[subsub:participatory\]](#subsub:participatory){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsub:participatory"}. However, politically, most model
developers lack incentives to share control with communities
[@gabriel2020artificial]. Current alignment pipelines are centralized by
the small set of companies with resources to develop LLMs. Similarly,
academic institutions and governments can serve to centralize
decision-making across the LLM development pipeline
[@suresh2024participation]. There are a number of less centralized
alternatives. For example, Masakhane [@orife2020masakhane] is a network
of NLP researchers working on NLP for local African languages, with
community involvement at every stage, from dataset creation and
annotation to model training. EleutherAI is a distributed,
volunteer-driven research collective that has created open pre-training
corpora [@gao2020pile800gbdatasetdiverse], models [@black2022gpt], and
scaling checkpoints [@biderman2023pythia]. BigScience was a research
effort in which over 1,000 researchers from academia and industry
coordinated through HuggingFace and built BLOOM [@workshop2022bloom], a
176B-parameter multilingual autoregressive language model, with
decision-making steps clearly and publicly documented.

These initiatives illustrate that steerability does not need to be
confined to top-down fine-tuning interfaces or proprietary alignment
pipelines. Distributed model development allows communities to steer
models from the ground up, establishing linguistic resources, value
functions, and development practices that ultimately shape downstream
behavior. At the same time, decentralization introduces its own
tensions, including coordination costs, uneven resource distribution,
and challenges of accountability. Open and community-led efforts may
broaden participation, but they must still grapple with questions of
safety, quality control, and transparent maintenance of HCLLMs. In the
following sections, we will discuss safety
([6.3](#subsec:safety){reference-type="ref" reference="subsec:safety"})
and interpretability
([\[subsec:interpretability\]](#subsec:interpretability){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:interpretability"}), as well as the tensions between
these objectives.

## Safe HCLLMs {#subsec:safety}

The third dimension we emphasize when building responsible HCLLMs is
**safety**. As defined in
[\[subsec:safety_eval\]](#subsec:safety_eval){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:safety_eval"}, safety is conceptualized as preventing
LLMs from producing undesirable outputs (i.e., those that may be toxic,
harmful, discriminatory, or dangerous), even when prompted to do so. For
example, the widespread use of LLMs raises critical concerns about
ethical and social risks related to their outputs, including
discrimination, hate speech, exclusion, misinformation harms, malicious
uses, and so on [@Zhang2022OPTOP; @bender2021dangers]. At the same time,
there are concerns that LLMs can be used as agents of harm, such as
using AI-generated propaganda for misinformation
purposes [@goldstein2024persuasive] or spreading information that can
facilitate harmful actions like the manufacturing of
weapons [@shaikh-etal-2023-second].

We begin by discussing the existing methods that are employed for
addressing safety concerns both at the model training and interaction
layers. Looking forward, we advocate for expanding beyond this current
definition of safety, which focuses on preventing harms, to encompass
how we can build HCLLMs that also maximize user benefits.

### Current Approaches to Safety

First, we will discuss current methods for measuring and mitigating
safety concerns. *Red-teaming* is a common practice for identifying
harmful behavior through adversarial testing prior to deployment.
Red-teaming approaches differ across model providers, and details are
often not publicly disclosed as these practices are conducted in
industry settings [@feffer2024red]. As @feffer2024red survey,
red-teamers typically come from three pools: subject-matter
experts [@ahmad2025openai], crowdworkers [@ganguli2022red], or automated
methods, such as the language models
themselves [@ganguli2022red; @perez2022red]. The objectives for
red-teaming can range from broad mandates to identify any harmful
behavior to targeted assessments of specific risks, such as those
related to national security. After deployment, model providers may also
run bug bounty programs that offer incentives for discovering safety or
security
vulnerabilities [@openai2025_gpt5_bio_bug_bounty; @anthropic2025_model_safety_bug_bounty].
In addition to red-teaming efforts, model developers make use of
benchmarks and other safety evaluations, which we discuss in detail in
[\[subsec:safety_eval\]](#subsec:safety_eval){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:safety_eval"}.

Mitigations can appear at various stages of the model development
pipeline. At the pre-training phase, there is interest in filtering
datasets to remove toxic content as a preventative
safeguard [@obrien2025deepignorance; @mendu2025towards; @stranisci2025they].
At the same time, other work has argued that filtering toxic data during
pre-training can have detrimental downstream effects, and that including
such data at pre-training can actually make these behaviors easier to
remove through
fine-tuning [@li2025bad; @maini2025safety; @longpre-etal-2024-pretrainers].
Many efforts also address safety concerns during post-training.
Foundational techniques for modern LLMs, such as RLHF, are useful not
only for increasing model helpfulness but also for aligning models to be
more harmless [@ouyang2022training]. Building on these principles,
additional post-training methods can help automate parts of this
process. For instance, Constitutional AI allows researchers to
pre-determine a set of ethical principles for the model to adhere
to [@bai2022constitutional]. Instruction-tuning methods can also reduce
toxicity (see
[\[subsubsec:succeses_instruction_tuning\]](#subsubsec:succeses_instruction_tuning){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsubsec:succeses_instruction_tuning"}). Once deployed,
guardrail models are used to help moderate both user inputs and
generated outputs [@inan2023llama; @dong2024building; @rebedea2023nemo].

### Looking Forward

Like other human-centered objectives, *safety* can be an underspecified,
ambiguous, or contested target. As we anticipate the development of more
human-centered LLMs, we should be asking whose definitions of safety are
prioritized, and how we can design models that not only prevent harm but
can actively promote user flourishing.

#### Paying heed to long-term harms.

As surveyed above, existing AI safety research tends to focus on
immediate harms that users face when interacting with models, such as
exposure to toxic speech or the production of misinformation. Of course,
these harms carry long-term societal consequences. However, an
underexplored class of safety problems involves behavior that appears
innocuous in the short term but can compound over repeated usage to
become problematic. The recent work in this vein has identified specific
model properties, such as sycophancy, which can affect users'
psychological states and behaviors [@cheng2025sycophantic]. An open
challenge lies in measuring these long-term interaction harms, as they
are difficult to capture with standard evaluation practices like
benchmarking. One alternative approach, as discussed in
[\[sec:hci\]](#sec:hci){reference-type="ref" reference="sec:hci"}, can
be to run controlled experiments to understand the effect of model
properties on users [@cheng2025sycophantic; @kirk2025neural] or to
conduct qualitative inquiry [@mathur2025sometimes]. However, this
process can be time-intensive and furthermore potentially exposes
participants to the very harms being studied. This concern raises the
question of what alternative valid methods exist, such as those that can
simulate these harms in silica. Beyond measurement, mitigations also
remain largely underexplored --- both in terms of interventions at the
model design and user interaction paradigms. Researchers have identified
properties that can exacerbate harms (e.g., steering models towards
being relationship-seeking in model design [@kirk2025neural], sending
emotionally laden messages as users try to exit a
platform [@de2025emotional]), but translating these insights into
preventative measures remains an important and open area for
exploration.

#### Expanding the definition of safety.

A second area of exploration involves expanding *whose* definition of
safety is prioritized. Definitions of safety vary considerably across
demographic groups, along factors such as ethnicity, age, and
gender [@rastogi2025whose; @ali2025operationalizing; @movva2024annotation; @gabriel2020artificial; @aroyo2023dices].
These variances are then encoded into models through alignment
processes, significantly changing model
behavior [@ali2025operationalizing]. Thus, instead of assuming a generic
definition of safety, there is interest in better capturing and modeling
the diversity of conceptualizations that exist. This direction presents
a natural continuation of the existing focus on pluralistic alignment
within human-centered LLM research. How do we capture these differing
definitions of safety? Some work has tackled the issue through
recruiting diverse sets of annotators to rate safety
perceptions [@rastogi2025whose; @aroyo2023dices]. Others advocate for
engaging with communities in a more participatory fashion to elicit
safety goals, which offer a richer understanding of how different
communities understand the potential harms of these
technologies [@qadri2025case; @bergman2024stela].

Despite the benefits of moving away from this "view from nowhere"
conception of safety, it is important to remember that communities
themselves are not monolithic. Disagreements inevitably arise about what
constitutes safe or harmful content or what model behaviors are deemed
desired or unacceptable [@gordon2022jury; @gordon2021disagreement].
There is a legitimate concern that implementing democratic methods could
inadvertently drown out the voices of minority groups. Yet this is not
grounds to dismiss democratic or participatory methods for AI safety as
a lost cause. As @zimmermanndon outline in their work, there are viable
paths forward for reconciling these tensions by drawing on practices
from political philosophy. As we move towards a more pluralistic
definition of safety, this requires thinking normatively about the
contexts in which we jointly maximize or balance considerations across
groups of people, recognizing that collective decisions may at times
conflict with individual desires or goals.

#### Considering not only harms but also benefits.

Finally, much of the discussion so far has focused on mitigating harmful
behaviors. However, we emphasize that avoiding harm is not the same as
maximizing user benefits. In pursuit of human-centered LLMs, we must
also prioritize building models that bring positive change for users.
This raises important questions about what beneficial model behavior
looks like, and whether our current conceptions of safety align with
what is truly beneficial. First, we must challenge the assumption that
"safe" models are necessarily the best for promoting benefits. As
@cai2024antagonistic challenge, perhaps there is a need to design
*antagonistic AI* systems that are "actively dismissive, disagreeable,
closed-off, critical, flippant, difficult, interrupting." Much like, for
instance, a student may be challenged by their teacher in the learning
process, when we design for benefits rather than merely minimizing
harms, the desired model behavior changes.

A second provocation concerns the scope of benefit: rather than thinking
only about the one-to-one benefit of a model on an individual user, what
about one-to-many benefits? We can envision designing models for
collective or group-level good --- for example, models deployed to
promote democratic health by finding common ground through
deliberation [@tessler2024ai], or models designed to benefit teams by
serving as collaborators within group settings. Just as there are
differing definitions of what safety means, there are similarly diverse
conceptions of benefit, raising parallel questions about whose
definition should be prioritized and how we reconcile conflicting views
of what constitutes a beneficial outcome.

13	Evaluation methods allow model developers, users, and stakeholders to
14	compare the capabilities and limitations of different LLMs, and to

69	## Model-Level Evaluations
70	
71	[]{#subsec:model_level_eval label="subsec:model_level_eval"}

73	### Benchmarks
74	
75	[]{#subsec:benchmarks label="subsec:benchmarks"}
76	
77	Benchmarking has long been a key driver in the development of AI
78	systems. Benchmarks act as a compass, encoding the values, priorities,
79	and goals of the AI research community
80	[@ethayarajh2020utility; @birhane2022values]. They help determine not
81	only how capable a model is, but also what we consider meaningful
82	progress, allowing us to compare the strengths of different models.
83	Recent research has argued for a shift in what and how we evaluate,
84	especially for human-centered applications. As LLMs increasingly
85	influence real-world decision-making, especially in domains like
86	education, law, healthcare, and customer support, the limitations of
87	traditional benchmarks become even more critical. Benchmarks must evolve
88	to better represent human values such as fairness, robustness,
89	usability, and positive societal impact. Below, we discuss a few general
90	principles for thinking about evaluating human-centered LLMs.
91	
92	#### Moving Away from \"Exams\" and Rethinking What We Evaluate.
93	
94	Traditional benchmarks often mimic academic exams, assessing LLMs by how
95	well they can replicate human outputs or solve static problems in
96	standardized formats like multiple-choice questions
97	[@hendrycksMMLU2021], math problems [@sun2025challenging], and code
98	generation [@jimenezswe]. While useful, this framing compresses complex,
99	multidimensional model behavior into a single metric. Even
100	interaction-based, human-voting evaluations like ChatbotArena
101	[@DBLP:conf/icml/ChiangZ0ALLZ0JG24] are limited by their brittleness or
102	their misalignment with how humans actually use AI
103	[@singh2025leaderboard]. In real-world use, LLMs are collaborators,
104	copilots, or tools embedded in workflows, so it becomes necessary to
105	evaluate them in natural, complex, and multi-step human-AI interaction
106	settings, not just in isolation. One promising alternative is centaur
107	evaluations [@haupt2025ai] where humans and models collaborate. Here, we
108	care about the outcome of the combined system. These setups get closer
109	to how AI is actually used in practice, whether it's writing, analysis,
110	customer support, diagnosis, or decision-making.
111	
112	#### Ecological Validity.
113	
114	A central challenge in evaluating LLMs for real-world use is ecological
115	validity, the extent to which a benchmark setting reflects the
116	complexity of how systems are actually used. Controlled evaluations may
117	offer cleaner signals, but they often fail to generalize to interactive,
118	user-facing deployments. Recent work [@li2025mind] has shown that no
119	single benchmark strongly correlates with interactive performance for
120	audio models across 20 existing datasets. A model that excels at
121	standard static tasks might still struggle in dynamic or collaborative
122	environments. This mismatch suggests a need for richer, context-aware
123	evaluations. One promising direction is to build evaluations bottom-up
124	from in-the-wild data. For example, @rottger2025issuebench evaluate
125	perspective and framing biases in LLM responses to natural user queries.
126	Benchmarks should also be robust and reliable, correlating good
127	performance with success in real tasks. This requires vetted examples
128	with accurate annotations and sufficient statistical power
129	[@bowman2021will]. Finally, effective benchmarks should reveal potential
130	biases, artifacts, and any dual uses, as well as ways to mitigate such
131	unintended consequences [@weidinger2022taxonomy].
132	
133	#### Data Contamination and Dynamic Alternatives.
134	
135	With LLMs trained on massive web-scale corpora, the risk of benchmark
136	contamination has become a serious issue. Many popular benchmarks are at
137	least partially contained in training data, making their validity as
138	evaluation tools less convincing. The line between training and testing
139	becomes blurry, especially for static tasks. This is one benefit of
140	dynamic, evolving benchmarks. Examples like DynaBench
141	[@kiela2021dynabench], Chatbot Arena
142	[@DBLP:conf/icml/ChiangZ0ALLZ0JG24], WebArena [@zhou2023webarena], and
143	WildVision-Arena [@lu2024wildvision] introduce a degree of human
144	involvement that better mirrors real-world interaction. Such dynamic
145	setups are promising for evaluating generalization and interaction
146	aspects and mitigating issues around saturation and contamination.
147
