9	# Case Study: HCLLMs and the Future of Work
10	
11	
12	[]{#sec:applications label="sec:applications"}
13	
14	LLMs are not only research technologies that a select group of people
15	examine, use, and probe. They have become a part of the lives of
16	everyday users, supporting tasks ranging from assisting with coding to
17	giving relationship
18	advice [@tamkin2024clio; @chatterji2025people; @yang2024swe; @jimenezswe].
19	For example, as of September 2025, OpenAI reported that their flagship
20	chatbot, ChatGPT, saw over 700 million weekly active
21	users [@chatterji2025people]. So, we conclude by discussing how our
22	considerations around the multiple facets of HCLLMs apply in real-world
23	applications. For example, are HCLLMs practically feasible? How do
24	HCLLMs affect individuals and what macro effects do HCLLMs have on
25	society?
26	
27	We focus this chapter on one particular application area: the future of
28	work. Of course, this is not the only area where LLMs are used; these
29	models have a wide scope of applications including healthcare,
30	education, political science, and so
31	on [@thirunavukarasu2023large; @adiguzel2023revolutionizing; @ornstein2023train].
32	Nonetheless, we focus on HCLLMs' impact on labor and the future of work
33	given public interest, as evidenced by the many headlines and
34	speculation, as well as the individual and societal level impacts that
35	models will have in this area [@shao2025future; @acemoglu2026building].
36	
37	The adoption of LLMs in the labor market has led to significant shifts
38	in human productivity, in-demand skills, and even possible macroeconomic
39	changes [@chen2025code; @eloundou2024gpts]. We will now show how model
40	developers can incorporate the human-centered principles from previous
41	sections to define, develop, and deploy HCLLMs within this evolving
42	ecosystem. To define HCLLMs here, we will first discuss *who* the
43	stakeholders are and how to account for these differing parties in
44	[7.1](#subsub:stakeholders_future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
45	reference="subsub:stakeholders_future_of_work"}. Then, we will cover
46	HCLLM development, how we ought to be training and evaluating models for
47	future of work purposes in
48	[7.2](#subsub:evaluating_future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
49	reference="subsub:evaluating_future_of_work"}. Finally, in
50	[7.3](#subsub:case_deploy){reference-type="ref"
51	reference="subsub:case_deploy"}, we conclude with considerations for
52	responsibly deploying HCLLMs, such as the potential for widening
53	inequalities or overreliance. The road map is visualized in
54	Figure [1](#fig:future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
55	reference="fig:future_of_work"}.
56	
57	![We present a case study on HCLLMs and the future of work, covering the
58	three key areas of defining, developing, and deploying HCLLMs. We start
59	by identifying relevant stakeholders
60	([7.1](#subsub:stakeholders_future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
61	reference="subsub:stakeholders_future_of_work"}), then move to examining
62	the model capabilities needed to better suit LLMs for workplace settings
63	([7.2](#subsub:evaluating_future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
64	reference="subsub:evaluating_future_of_work"}), and conclude by
65	discussing key societal considerations
66	([7.3](#subsub:case_deploy){reference-type="ref"
67	reference="subsub:case_deploy"}).](../assets/CaseStudy.png){#fig:future_of_work
68	width="\\linewidth"}
69	
70	## Defining the Stakeholders {#subsub:stakeholders_future_of_work}
71	
72	To understand how we can design LLMs for the future of work in a
73	human-centered fashion, we must start by understanding the *who*. Who is
74	being impacted by HCLLMs in the workforce? Is this the same group of
75	people that these models are being designed for? How might different
76	groups of stakeholders --- both direct and indirect --- be impacted
77	differently? There are many potential stakeholders, including
78	**workers** who directly interact with LLMs; **employers** who may be in
79	charge of procuring the technology for their organization;
80	**shareholders** who are interested in productivity or financial gains;
81	and **customers** who may see the final artifact or output created from
82	workers using LLMs.
83	
84	A natural group to start with are the **workers** who interface and
85	utilize these technologies as part of their work. Here, a recurring
86	theme is a fundamental mismatch between what people actually want from
87	LLMs and how those technologies are currently being designed. In part,
88	this misalignment can be attributed to organizational constraints, which
89	are more present in the work setting compared to personal use. For
90	instance, @nanda2025state found that employees frequently resort to
91	using personal accounts to access LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) as they
92	found enterprise deployments fail to meet their needs or feel too
93	restrictive. Yet, this workaround behavior is symptomatic of a deeper
94	issue. The way in which LLMs are currently being used in the workplace
95	is misaligned with worker priorities. For example, @shao2025future
96	conducted a survey with 1,500 U.S. workers to understand what tasks they
97	want AI agents to be used for. Critically, they found that the tasks
98	workers *want* to use agents for differ substantially from how tools are
99	currently deployed and where industry funding is going. In tandem with
100	the human-centered reasons for centering workers' perspectives, this
101	finding suggests that current AI development trajectories risk
102	prioritizing displacement over augmentation. Doing so risks repeating
103	dangerous historical patterns in which automation technologies lead to
104	displacement without commensurate productivity gains or wage
105	increases [@acemoglu2021tasks]. To close this gap, we must ensure that
106	the needs and desires of workers are incorporated into the design of
107	these systems from the outset.
108	
109	Taking into account the perspectives of **employers** or
110	**shareholders**, the question becomes whether introducing LLMs improves
111	the productivity and quality of work produced. What complicates this
112	question is the "jagged" nature by which LLMs are
113	useful [@dell2023navigating]. For some tasks, LLMs are particularly
114	performant and can automate existing process; some roles will see more
115	of a synmbiotic relationship where there is augmentation rather than
116	replacement; and in others, LLMs are in fact not capable at performing
117	requisite tasks at all [@mazeika2025remote]. There is a parallel
118	consideration around literacy --- whether workers are well-equipped to
119	use the technology. Harkening back to the "gulf of envisioning"
120	discussed in Chapter [\[sec:hci\]](#sec:hci){reference-type="ref"
121	reference="sec:hci"}, it is possible that LLMs may actually be useful
122	for workers, but workers may not know how to best specify their intent
123	or be unaware that such capabilities exist. This places a responsibility
124	on employers, organizations, and policymakers to invest in AI literacy
125	programs that equip workers with the conceptual and practical knowledge
126	needed to participate in an AI-augmented workplace, rather than simply
127	assuming adoption will follow deployment [@ma2025not; @nanda2025state].
128	
129	Finally, another stakeholder we will highlight are **customers** that
130	serve as another end-user in this setting. For instance, as LLM-based
131	systems increasingly replace human touchpoints in domains such as
132	customer service or healthcare, the impact on customers warrants equal
133	consideration. The evidence here is mixed: while interacting with LLM
134	systems offers speed and accuracy compared to human support, these
135	interactions can also raise frustrations around the lack of empathy or
136	potential for miscommunication [@huang2024can; @li2025artificial].
137	Furthermore, recent survey data shows that customers in the U.S. still
138	prefer talking with a human representative over an LLM
139	system [@customer2026]. This concern is heightened in contexts that may
140	be more high-stakes or emotionally-laden. Nonetheless, we also want to
141	highlight that treating this question of AI usages as a binary choice
142	between human-only and AI-only presents an inchoate view of the issue as
143	there is meaningful middle ground that leverages the strengths of both.
144	For instance, existing work has explored how we can use LLMs to upskill
145	professionals to offer better human support, preserving this human
146	"touch" in interaction while enhancing the quality of accessibility.
147	
148	## Developing HCLLMs for the Future of Work {#subsub:evaluating_future_of_work}
149	
150	Next, we discuss how we can apply a human-centered lens to training and
151	evaluating LLMs to enable a future of work that jointly benefits the
152	different stakeholders we have discussed. To start, much of the current
153	discourse around LLM systems emphasizes autonomous execution, or systems
154	that complete complex, multi-step tasks with minimal human
155	involvement [@shen2025completion]. Yet, focusing primarily on this form
156	of autonomous interaction, overlooks the potential gains for systems in
157	which humans and LLMs collaborate. For example, researchers such as
158	@wang2026position have raised exactly this concern in the context of AI
159	coding agents --- a domain where models are quite performant and has
160	seen significant adoption especially amongst professionals in this
161	field [@appel2025anthropic]. They argue that the field has moved too
162	quickly toward full automation and that human involvement deserves to be
163	treated as a first-class design consideration rather than a transitional
164	inconvenience. Taking this critique seriously requires asking what it
165	would actually take, technically, to build human-centered LLMs for the
166	workforce.
167	
168	#### Designing Models as Collaborators.
169	
170	One prerequisite is that models need to know *how* to collaborate.
171	However, collaboration is not simply a matter of adding a confirmation
172	step before a model takes action. It requires a more nuanced
173	understanding of when to act autonomously, when to defer, and how to
174	communicate uncertainty or request input in ways that feel natural
175	rather than disruptive. As @shen2025completion show, building more
176	capable models does not necessarily equate to better collaboration, thus
177	necessitating dedicated efforts. In fact, current training paradigms,
178	such as preference tuning over single conversational turns, can even
179	hinder collaboration abilities [@wu2025collabllm]. Furthermore,
180	successful collaboration does not mean indiscriminately putting a human
181	in the loop. While ostensibly beneficial, this interaction paradigm can
182	lead to unnecessary verification and inefficiencies that ultimately slow
183	down the collaboration process. The best form of collaboration will
184	necessarily vary, depending on the task at hand as well as the skillset
185	of the human and LLM involved. For example, sometimes the human may need
186	to audit the LLM's work; other times the right form of collaboration may
187	need to be a back-and-forth conversation; and in others end-to-end
188	execution by the model may suffice.
189	
190	To start, we must return to the core question: what are the ingredients
191	for a successful collaboration? In human organizations, a common
192	collaboration paradigm is *delegation*. At the moment, agents are
193	capable of decomposing complex tasks into more manageable units of
194	action. However, the next step here is being able to assign these
195	actions. Thus, we need to know what tasks to hand-off to these models
196	and which may be better suited for humans to complete or even to
197	delegate across multiple different models [@wang2025ai]. This delegation
198	capability must furthermore be adaptive across users, tasks, context,
199	and model
200	capabilities [@tomavsev2026intelligent; @guggenberger2023task; @fugener2022cognitive].
201	Beyond being able to delegate, there are many other proprties that help
202	make a good collaborator which are lacking in existing models, such as
203	proactivity [@lu2024proactive], transparency [@liao2023ai], and social
204	norm
205	adherence [@shaikh2025gum; @ziems2023normbank; @forbes2020social]--- all
206	presenting fruitful areas for future inquiry.
207	
208	#### Improving our Understanding of Workers.
209	
210	A second technical requirement is a richer understanding of the users
211	these systems are meant to serve. One push in this direction is
212	developing better user simulators which can capture the behavioral
213	patterns and habits of
214	individuals [@lei2026humanllm; @paglieri2026persona]. As our ability to
215	simulate users improves, a question we ought to return to is *which*
216	users are being simulated. At the moment, many efforts are concentrated
217	on generic user behavior or focused more so on knowledge workers (e.g.,
218	developers) [@naous2025flipping; @wang2026position]. This provides a
219	deep but narrow viewpoint of the workforce. The population of workers
220	whose jobs will intersect with LLMs is far broader, spanning domains
221	like healthcare, retail, education, logistics, and skilled
222	trades [@handa2025economic; @tomlinson2025working]. Developing better
223	user simulators for these contexts requires going beyond theoretical
224	modeling to gain a deeper understanding of how people are actually using
225	these systems in the real world. This is a genuine challenge, because
226	the most valuable behavioral data tends to be held by the companies
227	deploying models and is rarely made available to the broader research
228	community. Finding ways to bridge this gap --- whether through
229	privacy-preserving data sharing, partnerships, or the careful design of
230	in-the-wild studies --- is a prerequisite for building systems that
231	serve a broader swath of workers.
232	
233	#### Evaluating for Ecologically Valid Tasks.
234	
235	Finally, across chapters we have emphasized the importance of data in
236	the development and progress towards human-centered LLMs. To see
237	progress in this area, we must also have benchmarks that actually
238	reflect the complexity of real work. Many of the standard benchmarks
239	used to evaluate LLM performance consist of synthetic or highly
240	constrained tasks that bear little resemblance to the messy,
241	context-dependent, and often ambiguous nature of professional work. More
242	general-purpose benchmarks, such as GDPval [@patwardhan2025gdpval],
243	represent a meaningful step toward measuring model performance on more
244	ecologically valid tasks, and domain-specific benchmarks provides an
245	even more precise look as to how these models perform in settings such
246	as finance [@fan2025ai],
247	law [@guha2024legalbench; @li2025legalagentbench], and
248	medicine [@arora2025healthbench]. In tandem, we must also consider what
249	these benchmarks are failing to capture but that we may also want to
250	evaluate. For instance, how can we better account for how workers are
251	actually interacting with the systems or how the performance holds up in
252	the messy, open-ended conditions of real work?
253	
254	## Responsibly Deploying HCLLMs in the Workforce {#subsub:case_deploy}
255	
256	Perhaps one of the top-of-mind questions when it comes to the future of
257	work are the long-term societal impacts that these technologies will
258	have. How will employment be affected by the increasing popularity of
259	LLMs? What skills will be in-demand and which will be less important?
260	Deploying HCLLMs responsibly means taking into account these long-term
261	externalities now, and mitigating against potential harms before they
262	occur.
263	
264	#### The Paradox of Productivity and Work Intensification.
265	
266	A common perception is that integrating LLMs into workflows will
267	inherently reduce the volume of human effort. Initial stand-alone
268	studies looking at whether using LLMs improves how quickly workers
269	complete tasks show positive evidence: people complete tasks more
270	quickly with AI
271	assistance [@cui2025effects; @peng2023impact; @shen2026ai; @karny2024learning].
272	However, when it comes to the workforce, people are not completing
273	singular tasks in a vacuum. They must negotiate tasks with many demands,
274	coordinate with coworkers, navigate company politics, and so on. Thus,
275	when we look at the impact on productivity in a more holistic setting,
276	the impact of LLMs is less clear. Counter to the earlier studies, recent
277	work has suggested that rather than freeing up workers, LLMs may
278	actually amplify the intensity of
279	labor [@hbr_ai_work_intensification; @harvey2025don]. For example, a
280	recent study conducted by the Harvard Business Review observed 200
281	employees at a U.S.-based technology company, finding that LLM usage
282	promotes the phenomenon of "work slippage" in which AI leads to task
283	expansion and increased cognitive load rather than a net reduction in
284	hours [@hbr_ai_work_intensification]. This phenomenon is not solely
285	confined to the technology industry where LLM usage is more
286	prevalent [@harvey2025don; @johnson2025ai; @acemoglu2020wrong]. For
287	example, despite the purported benefits that LLMs have for educators,
288	using models often lead to more teacher time devoted towards validating
289	generated outputs beyond current time spent [@harvey2025don]. Thus,
290	instead of saving time, these tools may in fact create new tasks for
291	workers or potentially introduce friction into existing tasks.
292	
293	To address these risks, we provide two approaches. First, we argue that
294	the way "productivity" is measured in the workplace in light of
295	advancements with LLMs must be updated. Traditionally, productivity has
296	centered on output per unit time, capturing how efficient people
297	work [@mckinsey2025]. However, now that LLMs can quickly produce
298	outputs, efficiency-based metrics may be defunct. Instead, echoing
299	practices in existing work [@shao2024collaborative; @wang2025ai], we
300	call for broader evaluations that consider not only whether tasks are
301	completed but also the *quality* of these outcomes. More broadly,
302	updating productivity metrics to match the current state of the world
303	provides a more precise picture of how LLMs are impacting work. Our
304	second approach is to find methods that center workers' voices. Survey
305	efforts such as @shao2025future provide insight into what workers want.
306	Complementing this approach, we argue for additional studies that can
307	capture the "thick" descriptions of what users are experiencing, such as
308	through interviews or ethnographic
309	approaches [@geertz2008thick; @anugraha2026sparkme]. Such methods can
310	shed light on what is not captured through numbers alone, such as hidden
311	forms of labor, additional cognitive load, or coordination costs.
312	Together, these directions point toward a more holistic framework for
313	evaluating AI in the workplace that accounts for both outcomes and
314	worker experience.
315	
316	#### The Risk of Cognitive Deskilling.
317	
318	A second concern is the potential for deskilling, where reliance on LLMs
319	erodes the foundational expertise of human workers. When models handle
320	the "first draft" (or sometimes the end-to-end execution) of complex
321	tasks, workers may lose the opportunity to engage in learning processes
322	necessary to develop deep domain mastery. Perhaps in an isolated setting
323	workers may be completing the task faster, but they are also less likely
324	to learn transferable skills or knowledge that can help them in future
325	tasks [@shen2026ai]. It is important to note that these effects are
326	heterogeneous across workers. How someone engages with these
327	technologies matters: automating tasks wholesale is likely to accelerate
328	deskilling, whereas more collaborative, iterative interactions where the
329	worker critically evaluates, corrects, and builds on model outputs may
330	partially preserve or even scaffold skill development [@shen2026ai].
331	Another moderator is expertise level. For instance, novices may rely on
332	these tools more heavily and more uncritically than experts, which is
333	especially concerning given that AI assistance can impart an illusion of
334	comprehension without providing sufficient expertise in an
335	area [@messeri2024artificial; @shen2026ai; @macnamara2024does].
336	
337	These concerns highlight the importance of carefully designing how
338	humans collaborate with LLMs, as discussed in
339	[7.2](#subsub:evaluating_future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
340	reference="subsub:evaluating_future_of_work"}. For example, the risk of
341	deskilling can be included as a factor when considering how to delegate
342	tasks. In this vein, rather than framing LLMs as tools that automate
343	tasks end-to-end, systems should be designed to empower users,
344	supporting human judgment, reflection, and skill development throughout
345	the workflow. To achieve this goal, this requires intentional design
346	interventions that encourage workers to remain actively engaged with the
347	task, such as mechanisms that promote critical evaluation of model
348	outputs or structures that preserve opportunities for learning and
349	expertise development [@ma2025towards; @reicherts2025ai].
350	
351	#### Macroeconomic Divides and Digital Accessibility.
352	
353	Finally, the integration of LLMs also threatens to exacerbate existing
354	economic disparities. Traditional automation has historically widened
355	the wage gap between high-skilled and low-skilled workers
356	[@acemoglu2021tasks], but LLMs introduce a specific "productivity
357	divide" rooted in accessibility. Research into usage patterns suggests
358	that ChatGPT adoption is positively correlated with higher education,
359	high socioeconomic status, and residency in urbanized zip codes
360	[@daepp2024emerging]. If access to state-of-the-art models remains
361	concentrated within privileged demographics, the resulting disparity in
362	AI-augmented productivity could further exacerbate systemic inequality.
363	
364	Addressing this divide requires interventions at multiple levels. For
365	one, as open-source models grow more capable, this can help reduce
366	barriers to entry and broaden who is able to benefit from AI assistance.
367	However, access alone is insufficient. As discussed in
368	[\[subsec:bias_eval\]](#subsec:bias_eval){reference-type="ref"
369	reference="subsec:bias_eval"}, model performance and usability can vary
370	across social groups, meaning that some populations may benefit less
371	from interacting with LLMs even when they are
372	available [@hofmann2024dialectprejudicepredictsai; @hassan2025dialectic; @durmus2023towards].
373	Continued efforts to identify and mitigate such disparities in model
374	behavior remain critical. Finally, improving AI literacy will be
375	essential as a new generation of workers grows up with these
376	technologies at their fingertips. Educational initiatives that teach
377	users how to critically evaluate, effectively collaborate with, and
378	responsibly leverage AI systems can help ensure that the productivity
379	gains from LLMs are distributed more
380	equitably [@solyst2025investigating; @morales2024youth; @morales2025learning; @okolo2024beyond; @cardon2023challenges].
381

are more present in the work setting compared to personal use. For
instance, @nanda2025state found that employees frequently resort to
using personal accounts to access LLMs (e.g., ChatGPT, Claude) as they
found enterprise deployments fail to meet their needs or feel too
restrictive. Yet, this workaround behavior is symptomatic of a deeper
issue. The way in which LLMs are currently being used in the workplace
is misaligned with worker priorities. For example, @shao2025future
conducted a survey with 1,500 U.S. workers to understand what tasks they
want AI agents to be used for. Critically, they found that the tasks
workers *want* to use agents for differ substantially from how tools are
currently deployed and where industry funding is going. In tandem with
the human-centered reasons for centering workers' perspectives, this
finding suggests that current AI development trajectories risk
prioritizing displacement over augmentation. Doing so risks repeating
dangerous historical patterns in which automation technologies lead to
displacement without commensurate productivity gains or wage
increases [@acemoglu2021tasks]. To close this gap, we must ensure that
the needs and desires of workers are incorporated into the design of
these systems from the outset.

Taking into account the perspectives of **employers** or
**shareholders**, the question becomes whether introducing LLMs improves
the productivity and quality of work produced. What complicates this
question is the "jagged" nature by which LLMs are
useful [@dell2023navigating]. For some tasks, LLMs are particularly
performant and can automate existing process; some roles will see more
of a synmbiotic relationship where there is augmentation rather than
replacement; and in others, LLMs are in fact not capable at performing
requisite tasks at all [@mazeika2025remote]. There is a parallel
consideration around literacy --- whether workers are well-equipped to
use the technology. Harkening back to the "gulf of envisioning"
discussed in Chapter [\[sec:hci\]](#sec:hci){reference-type="ref"
reference="sec:hci"}, it is possible that LLMs may actually be useful
for workers, but workers may not know how to best specify their intent
or be unaware that such capabilities exist. This places a responsibility
on employers, organizations, and policymakers to invest in AI literacy
programs that equip workers with the conceptual and practical knowledge
needed to participate in an AI-augmented workplace, rather than simply
assuming adoption will follow deployment [@ma2025not; @nanda2025state].

Finally, another stakeholder we will highlight are **customers** that
serve as another end-user in this setting. For instance, as LLM-based
systems increasingly replace human touchpoints in domains such as
customer service or healthcare, the impact on customers warrants equal
consideration. The evidence here is mixed: while interacting with LLM
systems offers speed and accuracy compared to human support, these
interactions can also raise frustrations around the lack of empathy or
potential for miscommunication [@huang2024can; @li2025artificial].
Furthermore, recent survey data shows that customers in the U.S. still
prefer talking with a human representative over an LLM
system [@customer2026]. This concern is heightened in contexts that may
be more high-stakes or emotionally-laden. Nonetheless, we also want to
highlight that treating this question of AI usages as a binary choice
between human-only and AI-only presents an inchoate view of the issue as
there is meaningful middle ground that leverages the strengths of both.
For instance, existing work has explored how we can use LLMs to upskill
professionals to offer better human support, preserving this human
"touch" in interaction while enhancing the quality of accessibility.

## Developing HCLLMs for the Future of Work {#subsub:evaluating_future_of_work}

Next, we discuss how we can apply a human-centered lens to training and
evaluating LLMs to enable a future of work that jointly benefits the
different stakeholders we have discussed. To start, much of the current
discourse around LLM systems emphasizes autonomous execution, or systems
that complete complex, multi-step tasks with minimal human
involvement [@shen2025completion]. Yet, focusing primarily on this form
of autonomous interaction, overlooks the potential gains for systems in
which humans and LLMs collaborate. For example, researchers such as
@wang2026position have raised exactly this concern in the context of AI
coding agents --- a domain where models are quite performant and has
seen significant adoption especially amongst professionals in this
field [@appel2025anthropic]. They argue that the field has moved too
quickly toward full automation and that human involvement deserves to be
treated as a first-class design consideration rather than a transitional
inconvenience. Taking this critique seriously requires asking what it
would actually take, technically, to build human-centered LLMs for the
workforce.

#### Designing Models as Collaborators.

One prerequisite is that models need to know *how* to collaborate.
However, collaboration is not simply a matter of adding a confirmation
step before a model takes action. It requires a more nuanced
understanding of when to act autonomously, when to defer, and how to
communicate uncertainty or request input in ways that feel natural
rather than disruptive. As @shen2025completion show, building more
capable models does not necessarily equate to better collaboration, thus
necessitating dedicated efforts. In fact, current training paradigms,
such as preference tuning over single conversational turns, can even
hinder collaboration abilities [@wu2025collabllm]. Furthermore,
successful collaboration does not mean indiscriminately putting a human
in the loop. While ostensibly beneficial, this interaction paradigm can
lead to unnecessary verification and inefficiencies that ultimately slow
down the collaboration process. The best form of collaboration will
necessarily vary, depending on the task at hand as well as the skillset
of the human and LLM involved. For example, sometimes the human may need
to audit the LLM's work; other times the right form of collaboration may
need to be a back-and-forth conversation; and in others end-to-end
execution by the model may suffice.

To start, we must return to the core question: what are the ingredients
for a successful collaboration? In human organizations, a common
collaboration paradigm is *delegation*. At the moment, agents are
capable of decomposing complex tasks into more manageable units of
action. However, the next step here is being able to assign these
actions. Thus, we need to know what tasks to hand-off to these models
and which may be better suited for humans to complete or even to
delegate across multiple different models [@wang2025ai]. This delegation
capability must furthermore be adaptive across users, tasks, context,
and model
capabilities [@tomavsev2026intelligent; @guggenberger2023task; @fugener2022cognitive].
Beyond being able to delegate, there are many other proprties that help
make a good collaborator which are lacking in existing models, such as
proactivity [@lu2024proactive], transparency [@liao2023ai], and social
norm
adherence [@shaikh2025gum; @ziems2023normbank; @forbes2020social]--- all
presenting fruitful areas for future inquiry.

#### Improving our Understanding of Workers.

A second technical requirement is a richer understanding of the users
these systems are meant to serve. One push in this direction is
developing better user simulators which can capture the behavioral
patterns and habits of
individuals [@lei2026humanllm; @paglieri2026persona]. As our ability to
simulate users improves, a question we ought to return to is *which*
users are being simulated. At the moment, many efforts are concentrated
on generic user behavior or focused more so on knowledge workers (e.g.,
developers) [@naous2025flipping; @wang2026position]. This provides a
deep but narrow viewpoint of the workforce. The population of workers
whose jobs will intersect with LLMs is far broader, spanning domains
like healthcare, retail, education, logistics, and skilled
trades [@handa2025economic; @tomlinson2025working]. Developing better
user simulators for these contexts requires going beyond theoretical
modeling to gain a deeper understanding of how people are actually using
these systems in the real world. This is a genuine challenge, because
the most valuable behavioral data tends to be held by the companies
deploying models and is rarely made available to the broader research
community. Finding ways to bridge this gap --- whether through
privacy-preserving data sharing, partnerships, or the careful design of
in-the-wild studies --- is a prerequisite for building systems that
serve a broader swath of workers.

#### Evaluating for Ecologically Valid Tasks.

Finally, across chapters we have emphasized the importance of data in
the development and progress towards human-centered LLMs. To see
progress in this area, we must also have benchmarks that actually
reflect the complexity of real work. Many of the standard benchmarks
used to evaluate LLM performance consist of synthetic or highly
constrained tasks that bear little resemblance to the messy,
context-dependent, and often ambiguous nature of professional work. More
general-purpose benchmarks, such as GDPval [@patwardhan2025gdpval],
represent a meaningful step toward measuring model performance on more
ecologically valid tasks, and domain-specific benchmarks provides an
even more precise look as to how these models perform in settings such
as finance [@fan2025ai],
law [@guha2024legalbench; @li2025legalagentbench], and
medicine [@arora2025healthbench]. In tandem, we must also consider what
these benchmarks are failing to capture but that we may also want to
evaluate. For instance, how can we better account for how workers are
actually interacting with the systems or how the performance holds up in
the messy, open-ended conditions of real work?

## Responsibly Deploying HCLLMs in the Workforce {#subsub:case_deploy}

Perhaps one of the top-of-mind questions when it comes to the future of
work are the long-term societal impacts that these technologies will
have. How will employment be affected by the increasing popularity of
LLMs? What skills will be in-demand and which will be less important?
Deploying HCLLMs responsibly means taking into account these long-term
externalities now, and mitigating against potential harms before they
occur.

#### The Paradox of Productivity and Work Intensification.

A common perception is that integrating LLMs into workflows will
inherently reduce the volume of human effort. Initial stand-alone
studies looking at whether using LLMs improves how quickly workers
complete tasks show positive evidence: people complete tasks more
quickly with AI
assistance [@cui2025effects; @peng2023impact; @shen2026ai; @karny2024learning].
However, when it comes to the workforce, people are not completing
singular tasks in a vacuum. They must negotiate tasks with many demands,
coordinate with coworkers, navigate company politics, and so on. Thus,
when we look at the impact on productivity in a more holistic setting,
the impact of LLMs is less clear. Counter to the earlier studies, recent
work has suggested that rather than freeing up workers, LLMs may
actually amplify the intensity of
labor [@hbr_ai_work_intensification; @harvey2025don]. For example, a
recent study conducted by the Harvard Business Review observed 200
employees at a U.S.-based technology company, finding that LLM usage
promotes the phenomenon of "work slippage" in which AI leads to task
expansion and increased cognitive load rather than a net reduction in
hours [@hbr_ai_work_intensification]. This phenomenon is not solely
confined to the technology industry where LLM usage is more
prevalent [@harvey2025don; @johnson2025ai; @acemoglu2020wrong]. For
example, despite the purported benefits that LLMs have for educators,
using models often lead to more teacher time devoted towards validating
generated outputs beyond current time spent [@harvey2025don]. Thus,
instead of saving time, these tools may in fact create new tasks for
workers or potentially introduce friction into existing tasks.

To address these risks, we provide two approaches. First, we argue that
the way "productivity" is measured in the workplace in light of
advancements with LLMs must be updated. Traditionally, productivity has
centered on output per unit time, capturing how efficient people
work [@mckinsey2025]. However, now that LLMs can quickly produce
outputs, efficiency-based metrics may be defunct. Instead, echoing
practices in existing work [@shao2024collaborative; @wang2025ai], we
call for broader evaluations that consider not only whether tasks are
completed but also the *quality* of these outcomes. More broadly,
updating productivity metrics to match the current state of the world
provides a more precise picture of how LLMs are impacting work. Our
second approach is to find methods that center workers' voices. Survey
efforts such as @shao2025future provide insight into what workers want.
Complementing this approach, we argue for additional studies that can
capture the "thick" descriptions of what users are experiencing, such as
through interviews or ethnographic
approaches [@geertz2008thick; @anugraha2026sparkme]. Such methods can
shed light on what is not captured through numbers alone, such as hidden
forms of labor, additional cognitive load, or coordination costs.
Together, these directions point toward a more holistic framework for
evaluating AI in the workplace that accounts for both outcomes and
worker experience.

#### The Risk of Cognitive Deskilling.

A second concern is the potential for deskilling, where reliance on LLMs
erodes the foundational expertise of human workers. When models handle
the "first draft" (or sometimes the end-to-end execution) of complex
tasks, workers may lose the opportunity to engage in learning processes
necessary to develop deep domain mastery. Perhaps in an isolated setting
workers may be completing the task faster, but they are also less likely
to learn transferable skills or knowledge that can help them in future
tasks [@shen2026ai]. It is important to note that these effects are
heterogeneous across workers. How someone engages with these
technologies matters: automating tasks wholesale is likely to accelerate
deskilling, whereas more collaborative, iterative interactions where the
worker critically evaluates, corrects, and builds on model outputs may
partially preserve or even scaffold skill development [@shen2026ai].
Another moderator is expertise level. For instance, novices may rely on
these tools more heavily and more uncritically than experts, which is
especially concerning given that AI assistance can impart an illusion of
comprehension without providing sufficient expertise in an
area [@messeri2024artificial; @shen2026ai; @macnamara2024does].

These concerns highlight the importance of carefully designing how
humans collaborate with LLMs, as discussed in
[7.2](#subsub:evaluating_future_of_work){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsub:evaluating_future_of_work"}. For example, the risk of
deskilling can be included as a factor when considering how to delegate
tasks. In this vein, rather than framing LLMs as tools that automate
tasks end-to-end, systems should be designed to empower users,
supporting human judgment, reflection, and skill development throughout
the workflow. To achieve this goal, this requires intentional design
interventions that encourage workers to remain actively engaged with the
task, such as mechanisms that promote critical evaluation of model
outputs or structures that preserve opportunities for learning and
expertise development [@ma2025towards; @reicherts2025ai].

#### Macroeconomic Divides and Digital Accessibility.

Finally, the integration of LLMs also threatens to exacerbate existing
economic disparities. Traditional automation has historically widened
the wage gap between high-skilled and low-skilled workers
[@acemoglu2021tasks], but LLMs introduce a specific "productivity
divide" rooted in accessibility. Research into usage patterns suggests
that ChatGPT adoption is positively correlated with higher education,
high socioeconomic status, and residency in urbanized zip codes
[@daepp2024emerging]. If access to state-of-the-art models remains
concentrated within privileged demographics, the resulting disparity in
AI-augmented productivity could further exacerbate systemic inequality.

Addressing this divide requires interventions at multiple levels. For
one, as open-source models grow more capable, this can help reduce
barriers to entry and broaden who is able to benefit from AI assistance.
However, access alone is insufficient. As discussed in
[\[subsec:bias_eval\]](#subsec:bias_eval){reference-type="ref"
reference="subsec:bias_eval"}, model performance and usability can vary
across social groups, meaning that some populations may benefit less
from interacting with LLMs even when they are
available [@hofmann2024dialectprejudicepredictsai; @hassan2025dialectic; @durmus2023towards].
Continued efforts to identify and mitigate such disparities in model
behavior remain critical. Finally, improving AI literacy will be
essential as a new generation of workers grows up with these
technologies at their fingertips. Educational initiatives that teach
users how to critically evaluate, effectively collaborate with, and
responsibly leverage AI systems can help ensure that the productivity
gains from LLMs are distributed more
equitably [@solyst2025investigating; @morales2024youth; @morales2025learning; @okolo2024beyond; @cardon2023challenges].
